WHEN LEAD ACTS -LIKE STEEL.

Lead, according to Cassier's Magazine, is said to act like steel at ordinary tempera- tures when reduced to a very low tempera- ture in liquid air. It will serve as a helical spring, for example. This behaviour of soft, non-elastic metals is very interesting. It shews how very important temperature is. Just as iron is soft and inelastic at a high red colour, so lead is dull and soft at ordinary temperatures, for it is well on its way to be melted.
EVENING DRESSFS FOR GIRi.S.

SEWAGE PURIFIED BY ELECTRICITY. At Santa Monica, in California, has been installed the first apparatus in America for the purification of sewage by electricity. The method employed is that known as the Harris magneto-electrolytic process. Two large wooden tanks are provided with ten eats of electrodes, and ten clectro-magnets. The sewage is allowed to flow into these tanks, and cover the wires to a depth of 3in. A cur- rent of low-Yoltage and high amperage is then passed through. Oxyzan- and hydrogen are set free, the orga.nir matter is precipitated and ozone formed. The latter does the work of, purification, and the liquid, of ter passing through sand, appears as clear sparkling water. The cost for electric power is 50 cents for 1,000,000 gallons of sewage. THE SCIENCE OF THE FARM.

To the agriculturist and _ horticulturist alike there is probably, no subject causing more interest than the application of bac- teriology, the most recent of the biological sciences, to the oldest pursuit of the human race. It is little more than a couple of de- cades since scientists first began to realise the important part played by bacteria in aid- ing the growth of plants, yet so rapid has been the progress: of discovery in this sub- ject that a distinct branch of research, known as agricultural bacteriology, has arisen. The results already % obtained have given us a new conception of the funda- mental causes of the productivity and fruit- fulness of the soil, and have called the atten- tion of all " tillers of the soil " to the in- visible life which is constantly at work below the surface of our gardens and fields, and to the immense possibilities which may be realised by a better understanding of the ac- tivities of these minute vegetable organisms.

The papers were found upon him, and, since- deception was useless, Mrs. Armstrong confessed to stealing them. She had come to Stour Park for that, purpose, and both the nurse and the doctor were in league with her. Mrs. Ainstrong could walk as well as I could. She may have found real personal pleasure in ruining' Sir Francis's career, for, if she had succeeded as 4 tally as she hoped to do, she certainly would have ruined him politically. Sir Francis's apology to me was full and ample,' and paved the way for an interview I had with him' same little while afterwards. div.head: HARDNESS OF DIAMONDS.
div.p: THE HARDNESS OF DIAMONDS.

So hard is a diamond in, comparison to glass that a suitable splinter of diamond will plane curls off a glass plate as a carpenter's tool will plane shavings off a deal board. Another experiment that will illustrate its hardness is to place a diamond on the flat- tened end of a conical block -tf steel, and upon it bring arother similar cone of steel. If forced torthcr with hydraulic power. the _stone can be forced into the steel blocks with- out injuring the diamond in the least. The only serious rival of the diamond in hard- ness is the metal tantalum. In an attempt to bore a hole through a plate of this meta: a diamond clrill.was recently used, revolving at the rate of 5,000 revolutions a minute. This whirling force was continued ceaselessly for three days and nights, when it w.as found that only a small point, one-fourth of a milli- metre deep, had been drilled, and it was a moot point which had suffered meet damage, the diamond or, the tantalum.

div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.

PENKETEL The animal harvest thanksgiving services were held the'Peuketh Wesleyan Church oalilundlty. The build- -1,12g, which presented a very pretty appearance, had been "eccrated with corn, fruit, flowers, vegetables, Sm., by Eeveral of the lady members of the congregation. to ';`..llolc great credit is due. There waq a good congrega- n at the morning service, which was conducted by 'us Rev. P. W. Kernick, resident minister. The choir Le,ndered the anthem "Praise' the Lord 0 Jerusalem" th much effect. There was a good congregation at Tzi evening service, when Mr. C. Davey Smith occupied Rti!pit. The choir rendered the anthem "Ye shall Aweu In the land." Mr. Emk Ireland and Miss Connie therton singing the solo parts. Mr. George Weaver presided at the organ,

R. J. Peake. The sermons which were appropriate were listened to with every evidence of appreciation by the congregation at both services. The church had bon beanti°ully decorated for the occasion. At the evening service the choir rendered an anthem "Sing to the Lord of Harvest " (211anit1er), the solo being taken by Miss Violet ' Brown. On Monday evening a well attended social gathering was held in the schoolroom presided over by Alderman Ellison who introduced the newly appointed minister' the Rev. Thomas Gladding. Mr. Glaciding in a short specale expressed his pleasure at being present and meeting so many new friends and hoped that they would not only get on well together but that they world be able to report progress at the end of his stsy 1 with their A musical programme followed. Several ' glees and part songs were capitally rendered by the 1 choir and mile voice quartette party. Songs, which were greatly enjoyed by the audience, were sung by Miss Hartley and Messrs. F.Bleeso and Arthur Fletcher, whilst Miss Gertrude Ifenshall chatmed her hearers with a violin solo which was most artistically played. During the evening refreshments mere handed round , t,nd at the close the fruit and vegetables were sold, the ' proceeds going to the Trust Funds, whilst it was a pleasure to note that many of the vegetables &o. were banded over by the purchasers to the committee of the Benevolent Fund for distribution to the poor. BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHURCH.

Harvest festival services were held on Sunday at this church which had been tastefully decorated for the occision most of the work being done by the members of the Wesley Guild. The preacher at the morning service was the Rev. Blanshard Reeling, the newly- appointed minister, and there was a fair congregatior The evening preacher was the Rev. Thomas Miller, of Bold-street, who ministered to a good attendance. Prior to the choir rendered the anthem "0 God, who is like unto Thee ?" Mis S. Silcock singing effectively in the solo parts, Mr. Miller took for his text, " Hearken unto this, 0 Job, stand still and consider the wondrous works of God" Job xxxiivii. 14. The purpose of nature, he said, was not financial, it was religious. It was to teach us more of God and of man —of the development of life and beauty. They were said to be in a utilitarian ago, yet when they looked upon the world with a sense of awe how much it profited them ! They had got over the old Puritan's ! standpoint who scarcely dared to lift his eves from his book lest the grandeur of the scenery should cause him Ito forget such themes as predestination and the Isovereignty of the will of God. Indeed the qualifica- tion for a minister nowadays seem( 1 to be not • Can he I preach ? " but 'ls he able to lead an excursion to ' Switzerland ?" Only man was conscious in the presencs of nature that he was in the presence of God. A I sense of beauty should be cultivated. The preacher said ' he knew there were grumblings about the harvest, but I God's harvest did not cover our county or our country, ' but in the grane-ies of the world there was enough for all the sons of men. And if God looked after the , beasts of the field which had no reason, and clothed • the glass and the lilies, would He not look after them ? Was He going to forget them? He haew when their I homes were overshadowed. And if He watched over the plants that could not toil or spin, was He going to I neglect them ? But the fullest revelation of God had come through Jesus Christ, end in His servicl they I would find their chief delighi.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH LEGII-SrREET.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH LEGII-SrREET.

The harvest festival services in connection with the above place of worship were held on Sunday last The preacher for the day being the Pastor (the Rev. J. B. Buglass), who preached two inspiring and iusti active sermons to crowded congregations. The church was tastefully decorated with corn, fruit, end Rowers, a feature this year being two floral arches over the aisles, At the afternoon service presided over by Mr. W. Sherburn, Roots cantata " Esther" was rendered by the choir assisted by local friends as principals and the parts assigned were as follows :—Queen Esther, Miss A. Bridge ; King shuarus, Mr. G. Gough ; Zeresh, Miss Una Plinston; First Maid of Honour, Miss A, Woodland ; Mordecai, Mr. W. J. Booth ; Haman, Mr. J. \V. Warburton ; liigh Priest, Mr. J. Phillips ; Hegui, Mr. Alf Spruce ; Harbonah, Mr. Hodgkinson. It would be invidious to select any of the above for special praise as each sustained their parts admirably, as also did the chorus, all tending to keep up the ' interest of this biblical romance from start to finish. , Mr. H. Billinghara ably gave the connective readings. At the evening service tha anthem " And I saw a new heaven " (Pc ace) was creditably rendered by the choir, the opening recit being effectively srng by Mr. J. Willett, the double quartettes being taken by Miss A. Woodland and Miss It. Brown, sopranos ; Miss N. Woodland end Miss E. Spruce, contraltos ; Messrs. Willet and Phillips, tenors ; Messrs. Spruce and Hodgkinson, basses. Mr. Willett also contributed the sacred solo "A Man of Sorrows " with true pathos and feeling. The collections for the day were satisfactory being an increase on last year.—On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held in the schoolroom,wheu quartettes duets and solos were rendered by Messrs. N. and J. Woodland, E. and 11. Spruce, Messrs. Phillips, Watson and Spruce. The organist and accompanist throughout the services was Mr. A. W. Clatworthy, who carried out his duties with ability.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 3, 1908.

The mission iv.is tastefully adorned with flowers, plants, corn, fruit and vegetables. The choir rendered the anthem "All Thy works praise Thee, 0 Lord," Miss Bella Davies and Mr. A. Goulden taking the solo parts. Miss Standish presided at the organ. The service,was well attended.

div.head: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.

The harvest thanksgiving services were commenced on Thursday evening. The decorations of the church were most tasteful and reflected credit upon the follow. ing ladies who had had the work in hand:—Misa Davies; Miss Rigbey (pulpit), Mrs. Savage (chancel), Miss Garton and Miss Glover (font), the Misses Harrison (lectern), and many others. There Wa,. a fairly large congregation. The preacher was Rev. J. W. Baker, vicar of St. Ambrose Church, Everton, who based an appropriate discourse on tha words "Speak to the earth and it shall teach Thee." A feature of the masical portion of the service was the special hymn "The strain upraise, of joy and praise, Alleluia ! " Mr. Milner presided at the organ.

div.head: – HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.
div.p: - HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.

There was a large attendance at the first of the harvest thanksgiving services which WILI held in this church on Thursday evening. The church had been very artistically decorated with flowers, fruit and corn. The preacher was the Rev. W. T. Warburton, Vicar of Egremont, who drew some valuable lesgoris from the harvest. An anthem entitled "I will magnify Thee 0 God my King," composed by Mr. W. Johnson, of War- rington, was creditably interpreted by the choir. Mr. W. 2. Randall was at the organ.—The services will be continued to-morrow (Sunday) when the preachers will be :—Morning, Rev. J. J. Sandys (Vicar of Gateacre) ; afternoon, Rer. J. R. R. .loes (Vicar of Great Sankey); evening,Rev.Hon.C. F.Cross,Vicar of Stratton.

WARRING TON PARISE' CHURCH. The harvest thanksgiving services were commenced at the Parish Church on Thursday evening, when a largo congregation assembled. The church was beautifully decorated and much credit is due to She following ladies who had undertaken the work :—Mrs. Bottomley, Mrs. Fowler and Mrs. Scott, pulpit ; Mu. Collins and Mrs. Lunt, font ; Mrs. Cralk, Mrs. Looker, Mrs. Willis, Miss Spinks, Mrs. Lidvard, clergy stalls ; Mrs. S. Taylor, gasoliers ; Mrs. Farrell, Mrs. Brooks and Mrs. Price, chancel rails. The authe u " Fearing the Lord, be glad and rejoice " (by Sir J. Goss) was beautifully rendered by the choir, Mr. Poole taking the solo. The Rev. John ‘Vakeford, of St. Margaret's Church, Anfleld, occupied the pulpit and preached a very powerful sermon on the words" Then whose shsllthose things be which thou hast provided " (Luke xii. 20). He strongly condemned the folly of men who devoted the whole of their lives to the amassing of worldly possessions and gave no thought to matters of religion.

ST. JAMES', L ATCIIFORD. The harvest thanksgiving services were commenced at St. James' Church on Thursday evening. There was a large congregation. The church prasentei a very pretty appearance, ftuit, flowers and cereals being effectively used in the decorations. The preacher was the Rev. A. E. Meredith, Vicar and Rural Dean of Bawtry, who took for his test the passage "How many hired servants of my father have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger ?" It was a very effective sermon, and was much appreciated by the con- gregation. The anthem" Fear not, 0 Land " was sung, the solo parts being taken by Messrs. Jae l Dobson, John Eckersloy, Wm. Green, andl Pevitt.

div.head: MESSRS. PEARS9I AND KNOWLES.
div.p: MESSRS. PEARS9I AND KNOWLES.
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE COMPANY.
A PROFITABLE YEAR.

The 35th ordinary general meeting of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. Ltd., was held at the offices, Bewsey-road, on Tuesday, "for the purpose of receiving and passing the accounts for the year ending June 30th, and for trananting the general business of the company." Mr. J. S. Harmood Banner, M.P. (chairman of the Board of Directora)presided,and the other gentlemen present were: —Directors: Messrs. W. H. Blackly (deplity-chairnchn), John J. Bleoklv, Richard Brancker, W. Peter Rylands and Herbert 8. Bleckly. Shareholders : Messrs. J. H. Bowden, Ernest Cubbin, John Knowles, %V. Clarkson, Charles E. Bunch, R. Greenhalgb, J. T. Hatcpson, A. S. Blackly, John Blackly, jun., David Garnett, A. H. Burgess, William Richardson and John Temple and James Dodds (seoretau). TDECHAIRMAN AND TEIE COLLIERY DISASTER. EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY.

The CIIAIRIIIN, in alluding to the Maypole Colliery disaster, which occurred on the 18th August, said it was ascribed to Pearson and Knowles, though really it appertained to the Moss Hall Colliery Company, Ltd., of which Pearson and Knowles were the largest proprietors. The control of the Moss Hall Colliery had come under their directior, and he TAVI sure all present would desire to pass a vote of condolence with those who had lost loved ones in the accident. They who had the condncting of the Moss Hall Colliery Company especially felt the accident, because it happened tam) many contractors, firemen and other responsible men who were down the pit at the time. The suddenness and awfulness of the calamity had left a mark on everyone. There had been a strain on the health which it would take some time to get over. He moved a vote of condolence with the relatives of the deceased in their sad bereavement. Mr. W. H. BLECKLY seconded-and the motion was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN then said he should like to refer to the assistance which the Moss Hall Colliery Company! receive 1 on all hands from everyone in the district. (Hear, hear.) They had the brains of the district at their disposal as well as the energy and newest appli- ances which had been experimented upon in Yorkshire and Lancashire. These were placed at their disposal and they made what use of them they could. He was convinced that there was a great future for these appliances' though it was as well to state that they had not been brought to that state of perfection which made it easy to work with the rapidity 'which woeld tend more to their usefulness. At the same time they were very useful, and they were exceedingly obliged to those who placed them at their disposal. (Hear,hear.) He should like to refer to the exertions of their own men both at Moss flail and Pearson and Knowles. Their exertions were extraordinary, and most of them were men who had won their spurs at the collieries, and had won positions, but they did not hesitate to place their lives in jeopardy in their attempts to do good. (Hear, hear.) Two men Mr. Morris and Mr. Fox, performed a most gallant act in the face of terrible danger, twice going down the pit to rescue men who were in peril, and they hoped that Mr. Stephen Walsh, the Labour member for lace, Ur. John Knowles, and the directors of that Board would some time be enabled to obtain for those two men for their heroic act the King's Medal, as they thoroughly deserved it. (Hear ear.) He should also like -to refer to the able ser es of Colonel Higion, Mr. John Knowles, Mr. Ru ton, Mr. Arnie', and many others belonging to the staff who notwithstanding the fact that there was stile an element of danger in the mines did

div.head: COAL. _IN THE -MAYPOLE COLLIERY,
div.p: COAL. _IN THE -MAYPOLE COLLIERY,

which at the liberal turn out of a million tons a year, should give them sufficient to last the present generation. They were disappointed with the pecuniary results of the acciuent because it would delay the benefits which they might otherwise have obtained, but they were quite convinced that there was nothing in the conduct of the directors which the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iran Campany could take exception is purchasing this coal mine; becaire there was little doubt, if not this generation a later generation of Pearson and Knowles shareholders would be convinced that they had done a wise and a prudent thing. (Hear, hear). He would point out to them that this year for the first time when they paid the ordinary dividend they would deduct the income tax for this reason—that they thought it extremely desirable that capitalists who put their money in shares should have their attention called to the very serious charge of the income tax, and to the fact that apparently it and the death duties were to be the pivot on which the future expenditure of the nation depended. They did not find shareholders grateful when they gave them their dividends free of income tax, and, therefore, this deduction of the income tax would call attention to the fact that there was a body spending money in the most lavish manner at the head of the nation that wanted repression as regarded its extravagance unless it equit- ably adjusted the burden between capital and labour. The d vidend this year was a good one, as they would acknowledge, but it only brought up

It was, perhaps, forgotten that in the sixties a definite amalgamation between the L. and N.-W. Railway and the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway was agreed to, and the sanction of Parliament asked to a special Act to carry out the arrangement. The Bill was thrown out as contr iry to public policy. Surely what it was contrary to public policy to do by Act of Parliament 40 years ago, when the power of the railway companies was infinitely less than it was now, could not be in accord with public policy to-thy, if done by a simple agreement amongst tha companies in such terms as suited them. Ha thought that this was one of those questions that had been neglected and was in datrnar of going by default. Whether or not the present Government was capable of grappling with the situation and controlling it as the claims of the national interest demanded seemed a little doubtful, but if they failed to appreciate what was their duty, we were within measurable distance of the establishment of a geauiue American trust the result of which in the future no man could calculate. The resolution was carried. Mr. W. Peter Itylands was re-elected a director, and Messrs. Bleasa and Sons were re-appointed auditors. The usual votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

to 3 9-10ths or nearly 4 per cent. since the company started—not an excessive charge on a trading concern. No doubt they would hear comments like this: " Yon I paid a good dividend this year. Why has not labour got most of it But there was the average to be considered in showing what the net result of a good and prudently-conducted company was. He would not prophesy about the future. Mr. J. J. Bleckley could tell them more about it than he could, but, in his opinion, it depended principally upon the relations between capital and labour. The total sales of the company last year amounted to 0,029,000—0ver 25 per cent. (or £518,549), of which went in payment of labour to the men. The shareholders had a good dividend this year, but it absorbed £80,580. Labour took the first pull out of the puree, the shareholders took the last, and a rise of 15 par cent, in labour would have left no dividend whatever to the shareholders. In his opieion the complaint that was constantly pressed by Labour members of Parliament that labour did not get its fair share of the proceeds of labour was not justified by events; at any rate, so far as that company was concetacd. They certainly would not avoid bad trade and unemployment when prices were low if they did not make some protest against the greed which desired to absorb the whole of .the dividends which were distributed on carital. Their order books for coal end iron were on a lower level at tile end of the year thvi they had been for some years past, and he could only hope that peace would prevail and that they would get back to the times when even at lower prices—and they were quite content with lower dividends than this year, though they liked to retain them—they would be able to make a good return to their shareholders. (Applause.) The Chairman moved: "That the report and accounts be approved and adopted." FISCAL REFORM A TRADE QUESTION. HOW TO DEAL WITH THE UNEMPLOYED.

Mr. W. H. BLECKLY said at their yearly meetings he had repeatedly calk 1 their attention to the great mis- fortune it had been to the trade of this country that the subject of fiscal reform was made a party question —as it was a trade affair pure and simple. All their directors were fiscal reformers, not as politicians but C 3 men of business, and their convictions were due to their daily experience of the iniquitous unfairness of the present system of foreign competition. The country had now before it a condition of things such as employers of labour had seen steadily approaching for some time, and that i.vas the scarcity, and often the entire absence, of employment of large sections of our working population. To stem the tide of the distress and misery caused by that lamentable state of affairs we were having elaborate schemes of charity put before rs to help the unemployed. It was well known that to British workmen the idea of living upon charity was gall and wormwood, and lois experience of them was that they would not accept it until they were driven to do so by starvation staring them and their families in the face. instead of charity let employers ts in a posi' on, in spite of foreign competition, to provide their workmen with honest and useful work in the trades they had been brought up to. They heard of iron and stc3l works being closed or working short time all over the country, mainly be:muse British iron and steel was being driven out of our old and best markets, while the Government stood by and declined to do a hand's turn to assist employers to obtain work for their workpeople. India, which used to be one of our most valuable markets, was being wrenched from us by the help of the unfair advantagt • which foreigners had over us, not because we could not manufacture as cheaply and as well as the foreigr ors cool(' not because foreign work- men wore better than ours—quite the contrary—but because their home tariffs, which prevented us sending anything into their countries, eribled them to sell their surplus productions against us in what used to be our markets, at less than cost price. Our colonies, which ought to be our most important customets, had been snubbed and told that we declined to give them any preferenc 3in exchange for the most important prefer- euc3 they were anxious and willing to give us. Let this country take a leaf out of the foreigners' book and foster our trade with India rod the Colonies, and the present appalling dilemma of how to deal with the unemployed would fade away and leave behind it a con- tented and prosperous population, grateful to any Government which had the wisdom and courage to see and act upon the only method likely to b 3 successful. He seconded the resolution. (Applause.) I Mr. J. Tcotrr.s supported the resolution, which was adopted.

div.head: MR. J. J. BLECKLY ON RAILWAY AKALGAMATION.
div.p: MR. J. J. BLECKLY ON RAILWAY AKALGAMATION.

Mr. J. J. BLECKLY, in seconding, said there was one question ho wished to refer to which was one of even more wide-reaching importance, which, strangely enough, seamed to attract very little attention or opposition. It was the present movement on foot amongst the railway companies, which, if carried through, most result in a practical amalgamation of them all into one huge monopoly, governed by an irresponsible oligarchy of directors and railway man- agers, wielding the enormous power represented by more than £l,( )0,001,000 of capital, dominating the whole industrial position ; making or marring the prosperity of individual firms or whole districts, es seemed desirable to those who guided its policy—a veritable ' imporium in imperio" of the most dangerous character ; and a menace to all who de i ;tided upon cheap carriage for developing their trade, and to every c fticial or workman employed by that gigantic organiza- tion. In the coal and iron tra'de moderate rates and reason- able facilities were as the breath of their life, and the direct interest of this company in the question might be measured by the fact that the carriage paid upon material passing in and out of the collieries and works owned by it amounted last year to £144,000. He made those observations in no feeling of hostility to the railway companies, with whom they were at present on very good terms, and in whose future most of them were interested as Shareholders and investors. Nor did , he undervalue the many services they had rendered to 1 the country, which were patent to them all. But when it was proposed by a private arrangement to do away with free competition amongst them the very foundation upon which all the railway legis- lation of the country was built, and that which constituted the "raison d'etre" of every Act of Parliament under which they enjoyed their monopolies, he thought a company like their own, which would be so vitally and prejudicially affected by the change, was compelled to enter the strongest pro- test against the vnsunamation of the suggested arrangements. Whether a sufficient remedy could be found in strengthening and extending the powers of the Board of Trade—at present altogether inadequate .in their operation—for the protection of the manufacturing 1 interest and the publ:c generally, or whether the nationalization of the railways was the only alternative he knew not, but the que-ition was undoubtedly one which called for real statenrinship for its satisfactory solution, and in dealing with which mare opportunists' 1 makeshifts must land the country in the gravest disaster.,

div.head: FATALITIES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FATALITIES AT WARRINGTON.
LABOUREI KILLED AT BENSEY FORGE.

Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, held an inquest at the Warrington Police Station on Monday tou3hing the death of Joseph Thomas Bennett (30), 31, Green-street, who fell from a ladder whilst working at the Bewsey works of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd., last Friday afternoon. Mr. Armstrong, factory inspector, was present and Mr. F. G. Taylor, solicitor, represented the cornpiny and produced several photo- graphs showing the spot where the accident occurred. Elizabeth Ann Bennett said the deceased was her husband and had been a forge labourer in the service of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company for fifteen months.
Mr. Taylor explained the photographs to the Coroner, and pointed out that the roof of the building in which the accident occurred was being raised a number of feet.

Joseph Rathbone, ganger, said the accident occurred at a quarter to three o'clock. A number of men had been engaged for some time in raising the roof over the ten-inch mill. Witness had been up a ladder to measure the length of a girder and had come down again. In the meantime deceased had climbed up, unknown to him, and fell down. Deceased had instructions from witness to go up the ladder. To do the necessary work he would have to step on to a girder G inches wide and 16 iry.dr:s deep. It was perfectly safe to an experienced man. IVitness did not know what caused the deceased to fall. He was a healthy man, and as far as witness knew, was not subject to fits. Albert Bailey, -12, Kerfoot-street, also employed by the company, said it would be quite easy to got on the girder from the ladder. Deceased was stepping on to the girder when witness last saw him. Two minutes later Bennett fell. He thought it probable that Bennett was going up a higher ladder when he slipped. The ladders were quite secure and none of the runs were broken.—ln answer to the Inspector, witness said the ladders were secured both at the top and at the bottom. The Coroner said be was sure the firm always did the best they could to prevent accidents, and with such a reputation as theirs, be did not believe they would ever be careless in these matters.

The Foreman (who the jury had visited the scene of the accident) sr'd everything seemed to be in order. Ile thought the accident bad been Cfl USC 1 by a stumble. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." Mr. Taylor expressed the dcv sorrow and regret of the company that the rccident hr.l occurred. They would be much obliged to the Coroner for his rernarl,s with reference to their reputation. Everything possible was done to avoid accidents. During Mr. ‘Vntson's thirty-five years experience as a manager, this was the only fatal accident that had occurred on work under his control.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCTOBER 3rd, 19e8.

Congresses, international CULTURE AND and otherwise, seem to be DECADENCE, held mainly for the purpose of making our flesh creep. There is always some sensationalist with a dispiriting theory. At the recent meeting of the British Association one of the readers of papers accusal Governments of assisting the survival of the unfittest by making life more endurable for the poor. Fitness for survival, it seemed to be assumed, was to be inferred from a sertain degree of worldly prosperity. Why encourage persons who are not prosperous to increase and multi- ply ? A pessimist who surveys life from what we take to be the quite opposite point of view has been administering shocks to the International Congress on Moral Edu cation. The one thing of value, he says, is human quality, in which we agree with him. But this human quality, it appears, is being undermined by certain aesthetic principles which command a wide assent. We are develop- ing high qualities of mind and fine phases of emotion at the expense of the race. The broadening of our sympathies, our eagerness to protect the weak and defective, " the new passion of pity," are admirable in themselves, and con- sidered separately ; but they are nevertheless the cause and signs of national decadence. "Unless a change takes place,",says the latest prophet, " a few generations will dump us on the rubbish heap, and leave our place to a more vigorous, if more barbarous, stock." This is all sincere, no doubt, and it has at least a specious appeaeance of being scientific. We know that among primitive mankind the races which survived were not so much the strong in the head as the strong in the arm. The development of the intellect followed on the acquisition of a position of reasonable safety. The higher and finer qualities of the human mind had a pitiably small chance of expansion in the days when, as Mr. ANbnxw La.wo so concisely states the case, the successful and, at that epoch, the progressive races of mankind "dined upon oysters and foes." Yet we may fairly presume that the ultimate object of the purpose which governs the world was the strengthening of the human will in orderly directions, and the development of the mind and the emotions. The savage man with I a club, clad in the skins of bears, and making his home in caves, or holes in the ground, or huts on mountain tops, was without doubt the most fit man for his day ; but he would represent the extremity of unfitness for his environment if he were to flourish his club confidently in front of a Winchester rifle. He would much more certainly assist the processes of evolution by running away. Such special qualities as he possessed would then be most likely to contribute to human develop- ment. It may come to pass that the uncivilised races may again get the upper hand. Europe, said NeroLaoN, will become Cossack. That, also, is possible; but we see no reason to regard it among probable occurrences, any more than we see why, in any measurable distance of time, Europe should again be given over, to other barbarous races.

Dr. SLAUGHTER has his reasons, of course, for alarming us as to the future. He is not, to use his own excellent phrase, a mere calamity howler. He believes that we are slipping down an inclined plane because of the neglect of the duties of parenthood. It is comparatively easy to make out a strong case. The birth-rate of France long since fell below the level necessary to be main- tained for the keeping up of the population. There is a fast diminishing birth-rate in our country. On the other hand, we are sending away every year large numbers of representatives of the pick of our population. Ireland, which has been our right arm in the fighting of battles both on land and sea, is constantly being deserted by its young men. As to Europe generally, there is a constant stream of emigration from Italy, from Germany, from Sweden and Norway, and at present more particularly from those eastern portions of the Continent which were formerly ,under the sway of Rome.' Taken over a wide area, the birth-rate is not satisfactory, the but swarms of children in the mean streets of our towns suggest that there is no very immediate cause for despair among ourselves. If we are preparing the way for the incoming of the barbarian, it is not at a pace which at present furnishes occasion for, any extensive alarm.

On Thursday the General To IlmvEnsan Post Office dealt with the PENNY PosTeon. first penny postage to the United States. The first sailing took place yesterday, when the Lusitania left Liverpool. Penny postage in the Empire and between this country and America has been the growth of a decade, and it is a question now how ion" it will be before it reaches general appli- cation. The significant fact is that while 'fifty million letters are posted annually from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign countries at the higher rate, the actual increase of letters posted and delivered in Great Britain itself is twice as many. The comparison is the more striking when it is remembered that the number of letters delivered in the United Kingdom last year was 2,800 millions. As Mr. Henniker Heaton says in the "Nineteenth Century," the total sent abroad annually at the higher rate is "merely a drop in the Ocean.' It was on Christmas Day, 1898, that imperial penny postage was inaugurated, and the returns show that so great has been the increase of traffic that revenue, as a consequence, has gone up instead of going down. A total of 28,000 letters was sent to Canada in the week preceding penny postage, but

in eight years after the number of letters had quadrupled. An enormous increase of postage with the United States is bound to accrue. India and Natal were included in the first scheme, but to the Orange Rwar Colony, the Transvaal, and New Zealand since MO, and Australia since 1905, the outgoing mails have been greatly augmented by the substitution of the penny rate for the previous 211. The new understanding with the States will probably produce the most dramatic development of all.
Mr. A. H. Crosfield, MR. CROSFIELD AND delivered a speech of UNEMPLOYMENT. considerable interest and

importance at the social' gathering held at the Liberal Club on Thursday evening, and we would commend his remarks to the thoughtful perusal of our readers. At present the all important question is that of unemploy- ment and the Borough Member did not hesitate to deal with it in a frank and thorough manner. In discussing remedies,he rightly pointed out that it would be impossible to find an immolate solu tion in one sweeping measure. Various courses can, however, be adopted materially to reduce the evil and two of them to which Mr. Crosfield attached considerable importance were Mr. Ilaldane's offer to provide military training for 16,000 or 17;000 of the able-bodied youth of the country in order to tide them over the winter months, and the pro posal that employers of labour who find their business affected by the wave of depression should resort to shorter hours rather than to wholesale discharge of labour. We were particularly glad to note his criticism of the specious fallacies of the Tariff Reformer, and to hear his strong declaration in favour of the taxation of land values as the greatest cure for unemployment. Mr. Crosfield has hit the principal nail right on the head, and we are sure all progressives will be ready to give him a hearty backing in his advocacy of this great and pressing reform. It is nothing short of a scandal that landlords should be allowed to hold up land in the neighbourhood of our large towns and cities for purely speculative purposes without making any adequate return to the exchequer in the way of taxation. Progress is impeded and slumdom perpetuated by this selfish policy and Mr. Crosfield clearly showed that by removing the injustice the Government would confer a double boon upon the community, in that industrial interprise would be fostered and productive work would be found for great numbers of those who at present seem to get elbowed out of the ranks in the grim struggle for existence. We hope the present Government will, before it surrenders the reins of office, apply itself determinedly to the solution of the land problem, which lies at the 'root of all social progress.

There have been many How THE LINV. famous telegrams in history, ABIDING SUBJCCTS some of which while coming PROTESTED, from the seat of war have not been remarkable for their veracity. Some of them have described events which never took place; and others have furniEhed equally unreliable descriptions of things seen through coloured glasses. Akin to one of these types of telegrams is that alleged to have been sent to the " Observer " office on Sanday from Hyde Park, and a copy of which has been generously printed and posted on the hoardings of Warrington. div.p: ARE HERE PROTESTINE AGAINST THE RIGHTS OF
ENGLISHMEN being CONFISCATED.

Wo do not know whether the " Observer " people broke the Sabbath by keeping their office open specially on Sunday in order to receive the above dispatch from the front, but we don't think they did. Anyhow, there it is —on every public- house front as well as the hoardings—so it must have been sent, must it not ? It was a very thoughtful act on the part of someone, and dispelled, like a gleam of sunshine through the mist, all doubts which may have been held as to whether, for instance, Hyde Park was filled by law-abiding subjects or not: The message says that hundreds of thousands of them were there, on the spot, " protesting against the rights of Englishmen being confiscated." These words conjure up a mental picture of simple grandeur. We can see them, these law-abiding subjects, " protesting" with heart and voice on this Sabbath afternoon against their rights being confiscated. It was truly noble , of them, and if we inquired no further we might deem them worthy of inclusion in a future edition of Fox's "Book of Martyrs." But truth compels us to add that this famous telegram does not tell all the story. Possibly it conveys all that its writer saw, but other correspondents have supplied details which fill in the gaps. The rights which were being confiscated—what were they? Why the rights of the free Briton to drink " beer, beer, glorious beer " without interference from a narrow-minded Government. And the "law- abiding subjects "in their hundreds of thousands— who were they ? Why, the employs of the brewers and the publicans driven to Hyde Park and herded like sheep until they emitted one united bleat which could be heard at Westminster. It was the poignancy of that bleat which inspired the telegram now on the walls. It sounded so law- abiding, but it was brewers' law. In the evening the protesting subjects got gloriously drunk also in thousands and were everywhere seen to be putting down their" rights " with a strong hand. The accounts of these proceedings has bean supplied in other telegrams, and -the whole is the tale of the great demonstration !

The Pearson and Inov.'his Tam PEARSON 114 D directors will soon earn KNOWLES MEETING, the reputation of being inveterate grumblers if they continue to .couch their public statements in such a pessimistic key when they have behind them the record of a year's remarkably profitable trading. What they would say if dividends dwindled to vanishing point is too dreadful to contemplate. This spirit of discontant seems to be growing on men like Mr. Harmood B inner, M.P. and Messrs W. H. and J. J. Bleckly—all of whom are usually considered to be generously endowed with this world's goods—and we are pleased to see that they have been taken to task this week for their lugubrious and fault-finding utter- ances at the Company's annual shareholders' meeting on Tuesday. The "Liverpool Daily Post ' rin a leading article says: "Continual croaking does not come well from the directors or a company that year after year pays off all sorts of capital charges out of revenue, steadily increases its reserve fund,and manages to pay its ordinary shareholders the very respectable dividend of 111 per cent."

Mr. W. H. Bleckly, as usual, complains about foreign competition and its "iniquitous unfair- ness." He wants a species of Tariff Reform which will enable the company to secure the monopoly of trade in certain foreign markets to the detriment of competitors in other countries. This he offers as a remedy for unemployment in England. We suppose it has not occurred to Mr. Blackly that the introduction of a tariff to meet his special requirements would inevitably have to be followed by tariffs here, thero and everywhere. Other people would doubtless see visions of cent, per cent, profits if only. the Government would build up a tariff wall too high for their com- petitors to climb over. This would involve Protection all round. It is conceivable that, for a time, the business of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles might boom—until say competitors abroad had raised their own tariff walls to a correspondingly convenient height. Then the last position would surely be worse than the first. We should havo unemployment with us once more, an' in an aggravated form. The battle of the tariffs would have reacted in other directions, par- ticularly on our supplies of food and raw materials, the prices of which would have

steadily risen as the virus of Protection infected gradually all sources of supply and demand. The unemployed would therefore be in the terrible position of possessing' very few shillings, and each shilling capable of purchasing considerably less of the necessities of life than formerly. It Is conceivable that the directors and big shareholders in concerns like that of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd., might in the meantime have feathered their nests to such an extent that they could personally view the position of things with equanimity. Bat their next step would probably have to be directed towards the ab)lition of the ruinous tariffs which were crippling industry all the world over. Evan big' manufacturers cannot both have their cake anu eat it. Triers is a natural law which makes such gastronomic eccentricities impossible of achievement.

y There is another matter about which Mr. Banner .., cornplains.The Chancellor of the Es2heqser insists, upon the company paying inoorne tax, and as this,, is a horrid charge, the chairman of the company thinks the shareholders should be made to feel it.' For the first time in the history of the company,- tberefore,the dividend is to be paid less income tax, not because the comp iny cannot ad)rd to pay the- tas, but in order that the shareholders may realise : that "there is a body spending money in the most : lavish manner at the head of the nation,"' and th3t. most be checked in its extravagance "unless it. equitably adjusts the burden between capital and , ,labour." " We do not know (says the " Daily Post '') whether all the shareholders in 6 Pearsori and Knowles ' are Tariff Reformers and fooa -, taxers, but however that may be, this barefac9d. introduction of politics into business is very dis- graceful To have directors of .e prosperous company airing their political ideas us this fashion year after year does not produce an impression that fiscal reform and a reduction of income tax are advocated in the interests of labour or of the community."

Liberals are looleng forward with keen interest to the visit of the Right Hon. Augustine Birrell, which Mr. Crosdeld has succeeded in arranging for November 23th. Mr. Crosfield promises other " big- wigs " in the near future and a politically stimulating winter season in Warrington is assured.

* We hope the brewer's telegram poster will not be covered up yet awhile. There is something humoroue about it which appeals to us immensely. The hoardings do not always provide one with a smile,, and as for the public-house fronts—well they are merely tragic.

* * * Councillor Pemberton has been honoured with the chairmanship of the new Towns Committee, which will in future meet once a month. We hope their deliberations will soon bear fruit, and that new indus- tries may be attracted to the town. A sum of £5O has been voted to the Committee for immediate purposes from the Walker Gift Account. * * * The Liberal Club looked like a miniature garden suburb on Thursday evening, so gorgeously arrayed was it with plants and shrubs. The occasion was the annual presentation of bowling prizes, and an attractive programme had been arranged in honour of Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield. It was the first official visit

of To—ro7field—tOili-e party headquarters and right warmly was she welcomed. The member has always been a prsona grata at the Aberal Club, but on Thursday he was quite eclipsed by his charming wife. There was a remarkable sequel to the debate on the King's Speech at the meeting of the local Parlia- mentary Debating Society on Tuesday. When the customary vote of approval was taken, the Leader of the Opposition adopted the strange and unconstitu- tional course of challenging a division. l',To wonder the Liberal Whip, Mr. Howes, called out " An insult to the King." This is a bad beginning for the new Opposition Leader. The Tories generally claim a monopoly of loyalty to the Throne and pride in the Empire. During the recess they must have become embned with the most revolutionary of Socialistic ideas, or else we must charitably conclude that they ma de a slip on Tuesday. * In the Town Council minutes we notice a resolution

of the Paving and Sewerage Committee which reads as follows: " Resolved, that the Committee visit the quarries of Mr. A. A. R. Lang at. Gourock." As the Committee consists cif ten members this resolution seems to err on the side of generosity. How mauy members found it convenient to take a trip to Gourock on the Clyde we do not know. Perhaps some Councillor will ask the question on Tuesday. We should think a deputation of three would have _ been ample for the purpose of inspecting setts. , Though, if it would result in some decent cubes being laid instead of the 41b. loaf abominations which ferns , so many of our streets, we should not mind the whole Council going to Gourock or anywhere else. ... * * 1 - We shall look for a few* electioneering speeches at . next Tuesday's Council meeting. As the Ist of 1 November approaches, Councillors usually display an ' uncommon anxiety to demonstrate the depth and '- sincerity of their concern for the ratepayers' welfare. In the agenda for the meeting we notice a batch of questions from Councillor Chantler relating to unpaved streets and passages and to the Warrington Bridge question. The Member for Howley does not often trouble the Council with either queries or comments, and his sudden outburst of activity now suggests that he has a feeling of insecurity about his seat. From what we hear the feeling is justified. Councillor Chantler will be very lucky if his repre- sentation of the Howley Ward is not contested. It i 3 nothing in his favour that he is a servant of the Trade! * * * Nothwithstanding the fact that Crypus has lost its Member' its prosperity seems to be advancing by leaps and bounds. It appears from the annual report , of the High Commissioner for the island that during. " the last five years the revenue has increased by 50 ' ; per cent: It is, the report declares, no exaggeration " to say that the island has reached a height of pros- = perity which has not been exceeded since the occupa- tion thirty years ago. Poverty as it is in England is , ' unknown. (It is in these times a relief to read of q prosperity anywhere.) With good seasons and the continuance of support from the home Government the Chief Secretary is confident that Cyprus will rank among the most prosperous parts of the Empire. We hope the " support will not be lessened in an degree owing to the absence from the House of Mr. R. Pierpoint. .* 5 * There has been some expression of condolence with the small tradesman with a post office attached to his premises on the rush of work consequent upon the demand of forms by prospective old-age pensioners. As a matter of fact the sub-postmaster is pleased. He has been promised by the postal authorities that every 'accepted claim" made through his office will mean payment to him of one shilling. Even a small proportion of accepted claims will pay fairly well, as one would hand out a good many claim forms for a shilling. The commission to be given for the paying out of pensions has not been fixed yet. But some pay is sure to be given, and an indirect advantage will also accrue. Old people coming, say, to a grocer's _ shop to receive the pension will in all likelihood i spend most of it in the same place in buying:/, necessaries of life, so the shopkeeper with a post office will not be badly off in the end.

_ * * * The sensation which was caused by the news of the sinking of the pleasure-yacht Argonaut off Dungenesti on Tuesday morning was intensified locally when it became known that several Warrington people were on board among the intending passengers to the Mediterranean. They were Mr. and Mrs. John Fairelough and Miss Marjorie Fairclough, -ryf Latch- ford, and Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, and it was e source of relief to all their friends when it beCaino known that they were none the worse for their perilous adventure, except that they lost all their luggage. With a fog in the busy water-way of this Channel there is always risk, some of it inevitable, la spite of every precaution; but, happily, when the kingswell collided with th e Argonaut the sea tras smooth, and there was consequently little comparative difficulty in managing the boats. It is only just, however, to say that the Argonaut sank so quickli that had it not been for the promptness of the captaitt and his officers; the discipline of the crew, and the calm and rational behaviour of the passengers, the rescue could not have been effected so easily. Special sympathy is due to the ladies on board, for even with ' a smooth sea it is not a very simple thing to climb UP or down the lofty side of a big steamer, and this feat they had to perform twice, owing to the unseawortbi- nese of the Kingswell.

Lundy Island, which is stilt unsold, not having fetched the reserve price, has strangly mingled early associations with hermits and pirates. It is extra- parochial, paying neither rates nor taxes, but belongs ecclesiastically to the diocese of Exeter, and the present proprietor, the Rev. H. G. Heaven, has hitherto officiated as parish priest for his subjects, like a modern Melchizedek. The legend runs that a late Low Church Bishop of Exeter, who voyaged to the islet f3r the parpose of Confirmation on a day • when Britannia had not ruled the waves very straight, threw up everything except his bishopric, and finally groaned : " I now firmly believe that we must pass through purgatory to get to heaven !" At this time • of invasion scares " it is interesting to recall that barely two centuries agke, Lundy Island was seized and fortified by the French. * The three Lancashire bands which won the chief Prizes in Cs Crystal Palace contest on Saturday have - all had sucesssful careers in the last ten or twelve , Years. The Irwell Springs band, which really comes from the source of the Irwell, as its name implies, ;yes formed over forty years ago, but it was not until 1901 that it began to challenge the position of the • champions in the band world. It was second both at •*he Crystal Palace and Belle Vii e in that year, and in 1904 it carried off the chief honours at both places, as well as the Nelson Cup and winning the Dancer' Shiald outright. In a tour in the South of England Crystal Palace Shield, which was being carried about for exhibition purposes, was nearly lost on the railway, bit happily the company concerned were able to intercept it before it reached the lumber-room to 'which it was in danger of being consigned. Crosfield's band, which came out second at the r, -Crystal Palace (says the " Manchester Guardian ") •is a newer combination. Backed by the Warrington firm with which it is associated, it has not had the •'struggle with poverty which Ir,vell Springs had in its early days, and in its seventh year, 1903, it Ivon no fewer than 22 prizes. Now it has apparently established itself among the best bands of the time. The Wingates Temperance band, which was third at the Crystal Palace, won the shield in 1090 anl 1907, and was evidently very near winning it outright this Year. In 1000 it carried off prizes worth R,1,410, and it has had other good years. Its home is a colliery Village between Bolton and Wigan, and a good pro- Portion of its players work in the pits.

[FROM OCR LONDON CORTZESPONDENT.] The interest of the Newcastle Election was scarcely great as might have been expected ; its imp artance, that of the Demonstration against the Licensing has been discounted in advance. The silence of tae recess which this year has been maintained more aausistently and for a longer period than usual, is over at last. Mr. Haldane made a notable speech on 'lnetuployment at Ladybank, and on Monday discussed tae Licensing Bill at Perth. Mi. Lloyd George on the ~anae day dealt with the Bill at a meeting of the North ales 'Wesleyan Synod. Mr. Runciman has been sPeaking on Welsh education, but contrived to steer lear of controversial topics ; while Mr. Walter Long aas displayed a good deal of unconscious humour on the subject of Tariff Reform.

THE LESSON TO LABOUR. There are indications that the Labour Party is ' ,awlikening to the impolicy of running a third candi- date who has no prospect of success, with the cones- luence that a Conservative is returned. Alderman ~„1-15rtley was not, of coarse, the choice of the Labour t'u'ePresentation Committee, which deprecated a -4angular contest under the circumstances ; and Mr. "• Brace, Labour M.P. for South Glamo:gan, has tointed out to a mass meeting of miners at Merthyr - 'ldyll the warning which an election like that of :`\revrcastle ought to give to Labour. Mr. Renwick, he ,renainded them, had always been an opponent of .Labour and of the Miners'' Eight Hours Bill, yet the _Labour vote had contributed to his return. The only reasonable course he declared, where there was no hope of getting a Labour representative elected, was to take the Labour programme and submit it to the rival candidateq, and then to throw the whole influence et ,the Labour Parts, into the scale of the candidate s Z4O was prepared' to endorse the largest pant of the abour programme. CONSERVATIVE INCONSISTENCY. That is a reasonable suggestion,and there is no doubt as to what would have happened at Newcastle if such Course had been followed there. At the same time lat Most be remembered that Conservative Candidates emetinaes hold themselves free to give pledges of a very extensive kind, individually, because they know tnat their leaders will never expose them to the danger ef being put to a practical test, When Mr. Gladstone taxed the Conservatives with their inconsistency in regard to the Miners' Eight Hours Bill, Mr. Boyar Law rejoined that members of the Party had been free act as they pleased on an "academic" question. The Liberal Government does not believe in treating B,oeial reforms as "academic questions," and there- ',..?re Liberal candidates do not lay themselves out, as `-'enservatives can, to catch votes by large and vague Teronnises. It is necessary for the Liberal Government consider how how far it can, as Mr. Haldane said at -4adybank, carry the timorous elements of the corn- ? Unity with it in its reforms. But this necessity arises mPly hecau-se the Liberal Government is determined f) advance. In the Conservative Party it is possible Or one candidate to hold out wild and impracticable r`2Pes while another denounces sober measures of eOrro as "Socialistic." It is possible, of course, efeaose the Conservative Party ha no plan or policy social reform at all. THE ONLY PRACTICAL PROGRAMME. LL't ig to the Liberal Party alone that the country can for a comprehensive scheme to deal with the Potoblem of Unemployment. The Conservatives can dler no better solution than a return to the bad old 143's of Protection and dear food. In the "Right to s Bill, which is the remedy put forward by the lilial:sts, we have at best only a palliative, though a aa n ative of heroic proportions in its costliness. And in Palliative applied to a social disease aggravates Lttead of ameliorating it in the long run. The lueral Government propose to treat the disease ,Lletead of the symptoms. A scheme which aims at riaPpling with the problem in all its aspects inevitably e4es some time in elaboration. SOME LINES OF ADVANCE. Haldane indicated at Ladybank- one or two of Ines along which the Government intend to approach the problem. A drastic reorganization of v"..e Poor Law system has for some time been seen, by oroghtful men, to be required, and the recom- endations of the Poor Law Commission may r;• expected to prepare the way for such a t erganization. Ur. Haldane foreshadowed some dis- i _n9tion in treatment between the deserving and the ,no,,serving poor. At present the chronic loafer, th t'esatute child, the aged and infirm, are all jumbled tegether in an indiscriminate mass which is labelled 'i.i.ePerism, and treated by the same crude machinery. (7‘.; Haldane also spoke of some inducement to be air-re dto the working classes to make provision ainst periods of unemployment. One of the most Ildelicate and difficult of the questions that go to make P 1 the Problem of unemployment is presented by the batuations in the demand for labour. It would pro- bl Le easier to finds remedy for the permanent Fittl4Plus of unskilled labour than for the intermittent rPlos of skilled labour. It is a point deserving of e most serious consideration whether this difficulty i'alnot be met, in part at least, by a system of State ,suraooo, In the meanwhile, there is the urgent call 14 eome immediate relief in view of the great pzeva- ee of unemployment. Mr. Haldane has found a _eetical expedient which, though it will absorb only ait_rafTall fraction of the unemployed population, will be e.oether beneficial as far as it goes, He states that yetilhe Prepared to offer to 16,000 or 17,000 able-bodied the fi /nen a period of six months' training during ea,. Winter. Mr. Crooks has welcomed the proposal as ° ef great practical use. A GREAT ISSUE. Th e immense demonstration against the Licensing gi.rei which took place on Sunday last, and which has statil. !IC) much occupation to the newspaper thji,t7"elans —the estimates of its size range from thousand to half-a-million —lost all its signia- i tai:_eee.because the organizers forget that it s the ray of those who take part and not mere numbers Ci eh give meaning to a demonstration. But the olrern their ,rnent are perfectly well aware that in setting rnaki.flands to this great social reform they are Itileg a considerable sacrifice of popularity. They Dew Perfectly well that they are driving away many therr'e who had supported them, and some even on aw,fl side in the House of Commons. It is per- direert to be expected that to the vested interests great Y concerned, the attempt to grapple with the htt tlaeat'il of intemperance should appear in any light tot t:of confiscation. But unprejudiced minds will e aellY be persuaded that the Government has

Timid Liberals may take comfort, if Temperance legislation seems to involve Seale loss of votes, in the reflection that, as Mr. Haldane says, "in the main the current of opinion in a great natioa makes for righteousness.' Mr, Lloyd George has reminded a Nonconformist audience that" Temperance legislation is not the kind of task that brings popularity to any Party, and n 3 Party would .ever undertake the job with any hope of alining votes by it." But, as he pointed out, the leaders of the Church of England have joined hands with Nonconformists in this cause, and if the Bill is thrown out with an apparent con- sent of the. English electorate—it means that in a question affecting the highest interests of the com- munity, the interests of the liquor traffic carry greater weight with the English electorate than the combined appeals of those who are responsible for the moral and spiritual welfare of the mu and women of the land. LORD TWEEDHOUTILPS RESIGNATION. Little surprise, but universal regret, was caused by the announcement that Lord Tweeduaouth's health compelled him to resign the post of Lord President of the Council. It had been known for some time that Lord Maeda:math:a condition was such as to leave little hope of his being able to resume the compara- tively light duties of his office. A capable‘admmis- trator, a tactful manager of men, an earnest and self-sacrificing Liberal, Lord Meal-I:loath has no enemies, and a vast circle of admirers and friends.

Lewis has resigned from the Berough Force after 18 years' service,and the Watch Committee have agreed to pay him a pension for life, out of the Police Pension Fund, equal to IS-50th's of his annual pay. ss. will buy a SAFETY RAZOR with 12. blades.— J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, 31 Bridge-street Warrington.—Advt. University Extension Lectures. In view of the exceptional popularity of the University Extension Lectures arranged by the Education Committee last *inter on the subject of " Plant Life," the committee have arranged with the lecturer (Mr. F.E. Weiss D.Sc.., professor of botany in the University of Manchester) to give a further course of six lectures on the same subject this session. The attractiv, nature of the subject, coupled with the interesting way in which it was handled by the lecturer last year, should suffice to ensure equal if not greater success for the approaching session. The opening lecture will be delivered at the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening next. Ancient Order of Forresters. The District Chief Ranger Bro. W. R. Smith paid his official visit to Court Kidd No. 475 held at the Horns Inn, Farnworth, on Saturday evening, accom- panied by the D.S.C.R. Bro. James Walsh, D.S. Bro. L. Davies and numerous members of the Courts of the district and the district officials, the journey being made by Mr. Greenough's conveyances. The D.C.R. in giving his report of the High Court held at Northampton, spoke at length as to the growing popularity of the Order and quoted various statistics and figures in support. After a very interesting discussion on the report a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Bro. Smith for the manner in which he had discharged his duties both as delegate to the High Court and as the D.C.R. for the past year. After the meeting the members sat down to an excellent repast, prepared and set out by the host in a manner which left nothing to be desired.

Committee. A special meeting pf the Warrington District of the Ancient Order of Foresters was held on Saturday last, the District Chief Ranger, Bro. W. R. Smith presiding. The action of the Town Council in refusing to entertain the election of co-optative members on the Old Ago Pension Committee thus depriving Friendly Societies of representation on that committee was warmly criticised and the following resolution was unanimously carried, the District Secretary being instructed to forward a copy of same to the Chairman of the Council :—" That this Warrington District of the Ancient Order of Foresters strongly protests against the action of the Town Council in excluding co-optative members from the Local Pension Committee and respectfully submits that representation from Friendly Societies is desirable and suggests that the Town Council recon- sider their decision with a view to making provision for co-opted members."
