div.head: Examiner Saturday, October 3, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, October 3, 1908.

The Government accepted an amendment by Mr. WILKINSON (Birmingham Central) :—" That steps be ' taken for the formation of a Board of Arbitration to settle all disputes and avoid strikes and lockouts." The CHIEF SECRETARY FOR IRELEND replied to the debate, and said that they were not at all surprised that the member for West Birmingham (Alderman Bennett) could only see in the King's Speech a skeleton, because he was so accustomed to looking at things through smoke-begrimed glasses. (Laughter.) The Government were at a loss to understand who was the leader of the Opposition, because the speech chiefly directed against the Government came from the menrber for West Birmingham and not from the member for Dublin University, who was said to lead. It was surprising how history repeated itself. (Laughter.) They had seen in days gone by how the member for West Birming- ham at Westminster had attempted to Pasert his superiority.—(laughter)--and if they could only be assured of the constant attendance in that House of Alderman Bennett, who represented that important constituency, they would be entertained to a repetition of what they had seen in the House of Commons in the past. (Laughter.) The Government were determined to go forward with their programme if there were twenty Newcastles every week. They would go forward and if they failed they would have the satisfaction of knowing they had done something to promote legislation which would remove those blotches which blemished the social conditions of the life of the people. (Applause.) A DIVISION.

When the vote in aPp-r-oval-Oriihe-liing's Speeah was taken a division was challenged by the Opposition Leader. Mr. HOWES (Liberal Whip).—An insult to the King. (Laughter.) Several Conservatives voted with the Ciovernraent, and the resolution was passed by 52 to 13.

Drowning Case. An inquest was held at Great Sankey last evening on Martha Cotton (20), of Margaret-street, Warrington. The evidence was to the effect that deceased was seen on the bank of St. Helens and Sankey Canal on Wed- nesday evening by a man named Hinchcliffe who shortly afterwards heard a splash. On g -ing back he could find no trace of the deceased. Later her body was recovered from the canal.—The jury returned a verdict of " Found drowned."

Musical Society's Opera. The bookings for the reserved seats in the Royal Court Theatre for " llerrie England " commenced on Wednesday ramming, when long before business hours people began to assemble and form a queue in Rylands-street From soon after S am, to well into the forenoon the bookings went briskly on and they have continued in a more leisurely way since. We are, however, asked to state that there are yet plenty of good seats to be had in all the reserved patts of the Theatre. Golborne-street BapMst Church. •. .

The first of a series of Gospel Temperance limelight services for the people was held on Wednesday even.- ing, a reading entitled " The man who spoiled the music " being effectively given by the Rev. R. E. Letheren. Recitations were given by Mrs. Letheren, Miss M. Freeman, and Mr. E. Whitfield. Solos were rendered by Hr. J. Hannan and Miss M. Muir. Read- ings, recitations and solos were all profusely illus- trated. Mr. Clatworthy ably manipulated the lantern. These services will be held monthly throughout the winter.

Animated Pictures at the Parr Hall. For the fortnight commencing Monday next, tie Parr Hall will be occupiel by the London Animated Picture Company whi.h plys a welcome return visit. There will be performances every evening at 8, with matinees on Thursdays and Saturdays at 3. A special feature will be a unique up-to-date exhibition of coloured and stereoscopic living pictures. Inter- hides will be provided by Helena Sleath and Charles Aldin who will appear in the Irish musical comedy act" Under the Shamrock," and their original scene " Dashing Duval : The Knight of the Road." Election of Guardian. - - - -

Tiro candidates have been nominated for the vacancy on the Board of Guardians in Howley Ward, caused by the retirement of Mr. Samuel Davies. Mr. Wm. Clegg, draper, 15, Salisbury-street, is proposed by Henry Leigh, seconded by Thomas Birchall, and in a 9ecoad paper the proposer is James Povey and seconder Stephen Moss. Tile other candidate is Air. Robert Lee, gentleman, (IG, Manchester-read, the propoger and seconder ou his irst paper being Jacob Sankey and John Gandy respectively. If neither of the candidates withdraws by 1:2 o'clozk on Tuesday next, the election will take place on Saturday, the 17th inst.

The Howley Foot Bridge. At the last meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee recommendations from the Bridges Sub-com- mittee with regard to the projected Howley Foot Bridge were considered and it was resolved that the next consideration of the whole matter be deferred until the next meeting, and that the question of the compulsory purchase of the lauds suggested be also deferred.—At the Council meeting on Tuesday, Alderman Ellison will move : That the site of the proposed footbridge over the river from Howley Ward to Victoria Park be within two hundrel yards from the weir.

Warrington Woman's Suicide. Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at the Police Station last evening touching the death of Ellen Carr (53), '2 7 , York-street, Latchford.—The evidence showed that on returning home on Monday evening decoaseTs son, Joseph Carr, found the front door locked. On entering the house by the back way he saw a bottle contaiomg carbolic acid on the kitchen table. He proceeded upstairs and found his mother lying unconscious on the bed.—lt appeared that deceaaed had purchased the carbolic acid from Mr. Yeomans, chemist, 137, Knutsford-road, on the pretext that she required it for lime-washing. Deceased's husband could not account for his wife's rash act.—A verdict of " Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was returned. Electricity Charges.—A Revised Scale. A new scale of discounts for consumers of electric light and power in Warrington has been adopted this week by the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee. The charge for electric light is 4d. per unit and the discounts will range from Is. 2d. to 2s. 2d. in the pound according to the units used per quarter. The consumer is entitled to the minimum discount on nsirg up to 250 units per quarter and to the maximum on using 10,900 to 12,149 units. 'For power the price is 2d. per unit for the first 1,000 units per quarter, and id. per unit after. The new discounts range from Is. in the pound for 2,500 to 3,749 units, to 2s. (ii. in the pound for 205,000 to 234,999 units.

Re-opening of Silcoates School. Four years ago the Slcoates School, a noted Voluntaryist foundation of the Congregational body near Wakefield, was destroyed by fire. Within the apace of about a twelvemonth, it has been re-bnilt,and on Thursday Mr. Walter Runciman, the Minister for Education, opened the restored premises in the presence of a large company of Yorkshire Noncon- formists. He was accompanied by Mrs. Runciman, to whom, acting on behalf of the boys, Miss Yonge, daughter of the head master (Mr. J. A. Yonge) pre- sented a bouquet of red and pink roses. The new structure is of brick, with stone facings, and stands three storeys high, with two wings. It contains a large assembly hall, with two class-rooms adjoining, provided with movable partitions. Immediately behind the assembly hall is a dining hall to seat 120. There are four class-moms, reading-room, and library, cloak-room, changing room, chemical and physical laboratories, lecture room, and music room. The dormitories will accommodate a hundred boys and staff. The building is in line with and resembles the Georgian architecture of the head master's house, which escaped the- flames.—Amongst those present wore the Rev. John Yonge and Mrs. Yonge, of Warrington.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
THE KING'S SPEECH APPROVED.

Budget Night Next Week. The enthusiasm of the members of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society has evidently not been fully re-awakened for there was again a meagre attend- ance at the second meeting of the session which was held in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday evening. Perhaps the night was not convenient to re my, but the change was unavoidable, the hall being required for other purposes on Thursday. The Premier (Mr. John Upson) was amoncit the absentees and his place was capably taken by the Chief Secretary for Ireland (Mr. J. F. Awbery). Mr. F. J. Taylor (member for Peter- field) undertook the duties of Clerk of the House in the I absence of Mr. W. Mason. 1 The CillEF SECRETARY FOR IRELAND announced that i the Chaacellor of the Exchequer would introduce the Budget next Thursday and two evenings would be devoted to the discussion of his proposals.Opportunitp would next be given for the introduction of a private member's Bill. ROMAN CATHOLIC GRIEVANCE. Several questions had been put in as a result of Mr. Asquith's action with regard to the Eucharistic proces- sion in London. In reply to Councillor Toole (North Monaghan), the Chief Secretary for Ireland stated : " I have been asked to summarize in one answer all the questions that have been put on this subject. I should like, however, to mildly protest against the assumption I in some of the questions that Roman Catholics do ' net enjoy absolutely the same religious and political freedom as all other classes and denominations except !in tho prohibition of the carrying of the Host. The i , grievance of the Coronation oath s not a disability. 1 Having said that, and seeing that the Liberal Partyhaa always been the party to remove civil and religious I inequalities we are prepared to propose the removal of the clause in the Catholic Emancipation Act prohibting the carrying of the Host, while at the same time regretting that the same tolerance and equality which are claimed by Roman Catholics in this country, are not extended to other forms of belief in some counties where Roman Catholics form a majority." Tas PATENTS ACT. Replying to Mr. Johnston (Durafries), the Chief Secretary for Ireland on behalf of the President of the I Board of Trade (Mr. JARM IN) said :—" It is perfectly correct that the terms of the Patents Acts tend to bring foreign manufactures to this country, and in no sense to keep them out. The contention raised by our honor- able friends opposite that it is a protective measure are erroneous. There is no industry protected by its means from foreign competition for the foreigner has still a perfect right to manufacture and to send his manu- factures here, but unless he is prepared to manufacture in the United Kingdom, he is not allowed the exclusive right which he formerly possessed to prevent our own manufactarers from making and competing for the Vadg if they desire to do so." ENGLISHMEN IN SOUTH AFRICA. Mr. W. L. WlLLtaoie (oswestry), on behalf of the member for Newcastle-under-Lyme, asked the Colonial Secretary if Englishmen were being displaced by South Africans in the Government of South Africa. In the absence of Mr. Furness, the Chief Secretary of Ireland replied :—" It might be thought from the way the Tories talk that out of every 100 Transvaal civil servants there were some 60 or 70 Dutchmen to 30 or 40 Englishmen. The fact is that out of every 100 there are no fewer than 80 Englishmen. This, too in a country in which there are, of course, enormously more Dutch than English. And the number of new appoint- ments since General Botha took office are 59 liinglish and 41 Dutch, instead of the 70 or 80 Dutchmen to 20 or 30 Englishmen that might have been expected from the proportions of the two nationalities in the Transvaal." DEBATE ON THE KING'S SPEECH.

The debate on the King's speech was then resumed. Mr. R. G. PIERPOINT (E. Manchester), in a maiden speech said the land laws under which we suffered were a crying shame and he hoped the Government would deal with that question in no half-hearted manner. The unemployed question was a complex one and must be ' approached with care. Neither charity nor unproductive 'labour would be of any avail. Then they heard the cry of Tariff Reform—from a party which had its ranks almost shattered last time it faced the country and which lost, out his very question, the support of such men as the late Duke of Devonshire. Free Trade was undoubtedly the best policy, for it enabled us to buy in the cheapest markets, and being able to buy the cheapest goods were would be able to reproduce the cheapest manufactured article. The imposition of tariffs meant bolstering up weak trades and putting a tax on the purchaser. The fiscal policy was brought forward by a party which caused the Transvaal war— (cries of "No, no,")—which cost this country £250,000,009 and the loss of many valuable lives. Workingmen would do well to beware of such a party —a party which dangled bright pictures before the poor, oppressed people of this country. He warned the Opposition that the people were becoming more educated every year. You can have your Newcastles and your Peckhams " declared Mr. Pierpoint, and the Opposition cheered. " Yes, rejoice in them now. You will reap your harvest later on." (Cheers and counter- cheers.) Mr. Pierpoint informed the House that he had worked in Germany alongside the workingmen there, and he had no hesitation in declaring that the position of the workingman of this country was far better than the lot of the German workingman. (Applause). Mr. HAWTHORNE (E. Belfast) said the Opposition did not agree that there had been any imperilling of good relations with Germany. They rgreed with the so-called "irresponsible " journalists that the best way of preventing bad relations was to be prepared to keep the peace. He welcomed Mr. Haldane 's proposal to provide 'for a large number of the unemployed during the winter by giving them a course of military training. The speaker roused cheers from the Socialist benches by expressing sympathy with the idea that one man should not have too much while others were starving. Mr. RIGBY (Scotland division of Liverpool) said the Nationalist members had nothing- but approval for the items contained in the King's Speech but there was one notable omission which the events of the past few weeks served to emphasise—the necessity for promoting legislation to remove Catholic disabilities. It was rather fatuous to suggest, as the Premier seemed to suggest last week, that some private individual should bring forward a Bill. That was a weak course and appeared to be an attempt to get behind the difficulty. He would appeal to freedom-loving Britishers to try and realize the insult which was offered to 12 million loyal citizens of the Empire in the Coronation oath. Councillor BALL (West Wolverhampton) in a neat and convincing speech, said that with reference to the deprecation in the King's Speech of the unnecessary violence and bitterness of a section of the Press in England and Germany, he would like to say that while two or three members of his uwn party had undoubtedly been helping to fan that bitterness he believed they had done so with the sincere idea that this country was unprepared for war. A large majority of the Socialist and the Labour party considered the writers referred to . . . . . . . . . .

Years ago ho and the doctor met with a severe accident while driving, and the deceased lost his nerve and had not since driven. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The Clerk stated that he had received a letter from Mrs. Carruthers, of Halton, resigning her position as a member of the Ladies Visiting Committee. A resolution was passed thanking Mrs. Carruthers for her past services and it was decided that Mrs. Greenharn, wife of the Vicar of Halton, be elected to the vacancy.

ARMY AXD NIVY PENSIONS. The Clerk stated that the Kettering Guardians had passed a resolution in favour of the weekly payment of Army and Navy Pensions. It was thought that the weekly payment of Old Age Pensions afforded an excel- lent opportunity of urging such a course upon the authorities and the Guardians were asked to approve the resolution and forward it to the Primo Nlinister,the Secretary of State for War, the First Lord of the Admiralty, and the local Members of Parliament. Mr. Wright moved that the Board endorse the resolution. De said he knew a case of a man in that House who had received a pension quarterly and had gone out and spent it all and returned. div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

OCCASIONAL COURT. At this Court, on Monday, before Mr. T. On:nand, Thomas SVinrow was charged with sleeping out. The prison pleaded guilty and asked to be leniently dealt with. Promising not to repeat the offence he was dis- charged.—Peter Syons was fined 2.5. CI. and costs for having been drunk and disorderly. STRUGGLE WITH A BURGLAR. On Saturday, at midnight, the night-watchman, John Higgins, employed at the Vulcan Foundry, whilst on his round of inspection, found that the officas had been broken into, and in one of the rooms he saw a man near the safe. Higgins captured him and took him to the lodge, meanwhile sending for the police. No sooner had the man gone on his errand than the burglar attacked the watchman, and in the struggle the watch- man was so badly cut with a knife, which the burglar used, that the would be thief was able to make good his escape. ,The wounded watchman was conveyed home, where his injuries were attended to by Dr. Lathom, and they were found not to be very serious.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH.

The Nth harvest home concert was held in the Lecture Hall, Lord-street, Earlestown, last Thursday before a large audience. The room was most artistically decorated with wheat, flowers and fruit, with here and there a gigantic vegetable, and the effect was beautiful. A splendid concert had been arranged for which some well-known artistes were engaged. In the interval the fruit, vegetablesaud flowers, all of which had been given by the congregation and friends belonging to the church were sold. The concert was a great success and the committee fully upheld their reputation for placing before the public a high-class programme.

div.head: Bold-street Young Men's Bible Class.
div.p: Bold-street Young Men's Bible Class.

The members of the Bold-street Young lien's Bible Class can fairly claim to have the best class room around Warrington, in which to discuss the many topics relating to the Bible. The room has been renovated and the re-opening ceremony took place on Thursday last. To celebrate this occasion there was a grand"' At Home." Several photographs of local Wesleyans, some of whom have passed away, now adorn the walls of the room. But the chief feature is a splendid photograph of those who form the class,which has been taken within the last few weeks. The size of the class may be judged by the fact that there are 53 who aro represented on this photograph. An excellent programme which was given, included the following artises : —Mrs. Booth, Messrs. Hickman, Weaver, Aahton,Pearson and Plumpton.— Mr. Holland, the president of the class, said they were met to celebrate the re-opening of the room in which the lien's Bible Class, connected with that institution, met on Sunday afternoon. The appearance of the room was a grand consummation of all their efforts. Old things had passed away and given place to new. In that room was a photograph of a notable group. Along with this picture they would see those of other friends whose memories they cherished and some of whom had gone to their reward. He would mention one which stood out in bold relief from them all. They had heard of his reputation; they had heard of the work he had done, and the good that he did whilst living. No other name would be held in greater reverence than that of Dr. Starkey Smith. Still they must make no comparison, for the work of other friends had been done well.—Mr. William Silcock unlocked the door of the room and was presented with a silver key for performing this oilize.—Several speakers spoke in eulogistic tones of Mr. Silcock.— Votes of thanks were passed to the artistes who had so kindly given their services for the enjoyment of those present.

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
Probable Contests.

There is every probability of a three cornered contest in Orford Ward. A meeting of the Liberal Ward Committee was held last evening under the presidency of Councillor John Wilkinson and the attendance included Councillor Cunnington, Mr. P. Peacock and Mr. J. Howes, jun. Mr. Peter Peacock was unanimously adopted as the candidate. Mr. J. Hampson will endeavour to retain the seat for the Independent Labour Party and Mr. J. R. Rushworth is the Conservative nominee. In the Town Hall Ward, where the retiring repre- sentative is Councillor Benson, Mr. T. Birtles, photographer, Legh House, has consented to stand as an independent candidate. A meeting of the Liberal Ward Committee was held last evening, Mr. P. O'Brien, presiding, and amongst those present were :—Councillor Locker, Mr. E. J. Mitchell and Mr. 3. Howes, jun. It was decided to support Mr. Birtles' candidature.

div.head: .NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: .NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.

By " Ovalist." Warrington have turned the corner at last ! Their first victory of the season was recorded on Saturday at the expense of Rochdale Hornets, and it was of so substantial a character that it left no doubt that the team was getting into form. The Hornets played a' very smart game, but Warrington were better in all departments, and scored 1(3 paints against 6. It was a capitally contested game,and until the rain came on, most interesting to watch.

Right from the start the Warrington men Went about their work with a dash which presaged their success.. Even Fish was " on his toes " and looking for opportunities, with the result that they came and he scored a couple of tr:es, one of which was worthy of his palmiest days. In fact, I don't think any other player but Fish himself could have got the first try. He ran right into the Hornets' nest—and out again. They were completely tricked just when they thought they had him. The home forwards played a rattling game, and gave the other six more than they bargained for, though the Hornets were no sloutches at scrum- mage work. Brooks and Jenkins thus had plenty of opportunities, and they mule the most of them. This was Jenkins' first appearance before the Warrington crowd since about the middle of last season, and it was gratifying to see what fine form he was in. As the connecting link with the three-quarter line he was splendid, and had a lot to do with the effectiveness of the team.

The locals were naturally much interested in the display of \V. 11. Dowell, Warrington's Welsh inter- natio4 forward. HO 53011 took the eye as a well- built, active-looking fellow, and throughout he played an untiring, game. He was naturally -bothered by the strange rules and strange surroundings, but he gave indications of proving an acquisition to the forwards. We have doubtless not seen the best of Dowell by a long way ! All the forwards seemed to play yell on .Saturday, but the best of the lot was certainly P. Boardman, who was in the forefront of every move- ment and also got a particularly good try. I can see this young player securing County honours like his brother ere long if ho perseveres. Another young player who showed up well was Hewitt. Lle did some rare tackling.

The bl-eks all worked hl,l Diciçopu in ~.^r.liC4l.ll. The eaptifTlP6ms to me to be doing rather too much and might part with the ball sooner. Cartwright shaped very vell, and Jordan was reliable but he is short of pace for a wing man. Warrington will hays to find a good right wing before the team can be Con- sidered strong on the attack. This has been a weak spot for a c3uple of years. Tilley gave another sterling display, and for a veteran he still takes a lott of beating. On the Rochdale side there was some good all round work put in. Young Hollingrake at full back fielded finely, and if he only had more power in his boots he would be a top-sawyer. The Pitalyes kicked too much, and seemed afraid to attempt to pass the Warrington pair. On the whole, the Hornets appeared to me to have a more promising team than for some years past.
Warrington have at last got a percentage of points to show, and now that they have got a foot on the League ladder I hope they will steadily climb upwards.

It will be remembered that the New Zealanders, though they could put a first-class thirteen in the field, were badly off for reserves, the bulk of the others being most " passengers " in a playing sense. div.head: BIG BEER PICNIC. --- HOW THE BREWERS ADVERTISED
div.p: THE BIG BEER PICNIC. --- HOW THE BREWERS ADVERTISED
THEIR STRENGTH.
An Argument FOR the Licensing Bill

The brewers' cheap trip to London took place on Sunday, and, as a means of enabling a large number of respectable working men and lads to see the town at-- 'prices below anything the railway companies would think of charging, it was a decided success. As a serious protest against the Licensing Bill, its ostensible object, it was the most pitiable failure ever witnesssed in Hyde Park. There was no heart in the thing from beginning to end, and long before the speaking was over, the real reason for the attendance of many of the demonstrators became apparent, for they wandered off in groups intent on" seem' Lunnon town" At no time were there more than 30,000 actual demonstratorvonnd the twenty platforms, and, if the number appeared to be greater, it was due to the presence of many spectators who had come out of curiosity and were not always respectful or patient listeners. They were for the most part a dumb and a somewhat shamefaced crowd, taking little interest in the speeches. THE WARRINGTON COITTINGENT. Warrington was well represented at the demonstra- tion. Two trains left Bank Claay station on. Sunday morning, one at seven o'clock and the other about five minutes past seven, and contained from 600 to 70a persons interested- in the brewing industry—the staff and corns of the workmen in the employ of Messrs. Greene!!, Whitley and Company, Wilderspool, and mem- bers of the Licensed'Victuallers' and other local trade associations. Easton station was reached at 11.30. Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint were on the platform and shook hands with many of the visitors. A procession was formed and it marched to Cardington-street, where it dispersed. The Warringtonians met again at the stme place shortly after two o'clock and marched to the meeting. The return journey was commenced at 1.21 a.m. on Monday, and Bank (Inv station was safely reached at about five o'cloak, A special train Tat the Central Station at 5.15 on Sunday morning and conveyed Messrs. P. Walker and Son's Warrington contingent; the local arrangements being under the care of Mr. Robert Hutton, head brewer and general manager, Warrington. London was reached at ten. Talc train and the Walker express from Liver- pool were met by Mr. W. R. Beck,the principal marshal of D section, who conducted the party to th 3 allotted point of assembly preparatory to marching to the Park. The trains on the return journey loft St. Pancras as follows :—For Liverpool 033, due 11.30; Warrington, 7.3, due at 11.13 p.m.

div.head: Beer and the Bran
div.p: Beer and the Bran

lAn article in the" Westminster Gazette " by Harold rs;C:2. discoursesoll " eer an i,bs; nrutP ,and symphonic association, the Sour of Beer expressel in drum-thwacks jubilant and aggressive." " The Drum I heard all along Victoria-street, whilst a procession, fresh from the railway train, marched to its measure. But Beer was absent, though symbolised in the hops that the proceesionists wore in their caps and button-holes. But in Grosvenor-place Beer mule its appearance. On the top of a 'bus, made stationary by the procession, a young man stood up waving a stone jar, and cheered. The procession took up the cheer, and even the Drum throbbed to a quicker measure when the young man on the 'bus-top passed the stone jar to the driver, and the driver raised it to his lips to the encouragement of " Up with a pail of it !" from those in the roadway. The processionists were encouraged by the sight of the stone jar. They were marching for a Cause, but a Cause is a dry and abstract thing ; and the hop-leaves in their button-holes, and the miniature barrels and pots that they carried pinned in their caps, were merely symbols ; and as there is nothing mystical about Beer or the worship of it, symbols must be, to the real devotee, unsatisfying •awl unconvincing. But the touch of actuality held aloft on the 'bus-top was a stimulation to their feet as well as an inspiration to the Drum—there was Beer, intimate and explicit, displayed above them—a little provokingly, perhaps, but, 13 till, there it was—a definite objective thing. And they marched with a blither step. They had seen the Cause— but concrete, in a bottle. And in Hyde Park I encountered Beef again. At the corner of the Ladies' Mile, where the crowd clustered at the railings to see the procession go by, a man stumbled to avoid an object on the ground, saw that it was a huge stone jar, frowned in his perplexity, looked accusingly at those near him, as if challenging the owner of the stone jar to disclose himself, and passed, bewildered, on. After all, a two-gallon beer-jar set comfortably down in the Ladies' Mile on a Sunday afternoon is a phenomenon rare enough to excuse a little surprise. The jar, however, was not without an owner. But she had at that moment, her back turned to it, and had not seen the danger it had escaped. She was calling to her husband, in the crowd before her. He turned to answer her, and plucked another man by the sleeve. The husband wore hop-leaves in his hair, wore his hat at that angle which we hare been told should warn the devotees of Beer "how far they have advanced in their dithyramb to the theme of muddle and fuddle"; and had a rosy countenance—" beery" would be a prosaic emendation, but the unpoetic truth. Bat he illustrated the joviality and magnanimity of Beer, for he plucked at the sleeve of estranger to introduce him to the stone jar. His wife, portly and cylindrical as the jar itself, immediately dispensed hospitality. The glass went nimbly round, host and hostess " drinking fair" with the guest. Then the guest—his hop- wreathedhat tilted at the same indicative angle—dived into the crowd, and squared the convival circle by making it a quartet. The new-comer he brought with him was a frayed and listless young woman, and her dull eyes became glazed with a dull delight when she saw a glass of beer unexpectedly thrust into her face. Nfanns in the wilderness—what was that to Beer in Hyde Park ! She did not illustrate the magnanimity, or the exhilaration, or the light side of Beer, but only its depression ; and entered the lists heavily handi- capped from a recent acquaintance with Beer. The other three appareatly started fair and fresh. And Beer, poured from a two-gallon jar, went round and round. And all the time the Drum kept going by. The hostess then began to extend her hospitality, and thrust out her relevant glass, brim-filled, to ask," Who's drank ?" of the general crowd, thereby indicating that those who had not might. And other men, with hop- leaves in their caps coming suddenly on an out-thrust glass of beer, drank it incredulously—and lingered. And gradually the whole benign process of beer was biographed before my eyes ; the listless woman became more dull-eyed ; the hostess became troublesome in her effusive hospitality (until a space about her was cleared by shrinking but fascinated onlookers); and the host, who wore a medallion in his coat with the words "Liberty " and " Honesty " writ large, began to reiterate this apothegm to the man, similarly medal- Honed : " Liberty you can't get. Honesty never 'ave." And the other man, nodding a drowsy head, solemnly agreed a dozen times. I evertook the host and hostess on my way out of the Park. They were linked arm in arm, singing, " Say an revoir, and not good-bye," and the host stopped his song, whilst his partner continued it, to ask the way to the demonstration. But, for myself, he was demonstra- tion enough. And, according to his lights, he had interpreted what the demonstration intended to vindi- cate and uphold."

div.head: Liberty and Licence. NIGHT SCENTS AFTER THE DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: Liberty and Licence. NIGHT SCENTS AFTER THE DEMONSTRATION.

Whatever value (says the " Westminster Gazette ") may be attached to the vote taken in Hyde Park in opposition to the Government's Licensing Bill, surely it was more than nullified by the discreditable scenes that followed the turning loose into the streets of London on a Sunday evening of the vast hordes of men of all classes—many, of them the mere riff-raff of northern towns—who, by cheap trips, free drinks, and monetary bribes for " expenses, ' had been imported to shout for beer.

Brakeloads of sympathisers left their women-folk in these vehicles whilst they went to the " scene of action," returning at frequent intervals to quaff mugs of beer, poured from gallon stone jars ; bands of roystering youths paraded the park with bottles of beer in their pockets, which they quaffed at frequent intervals, and to the song of Beer, Glorious Beer," and the phrase " They want to rob us of our beer whilst in many of the country contingents there was evidence, as their members danced and sang in the march, that the brewers-free refreshments had been dis- pensed on a very liberal scale. Indeed, some of the contingents brought barrels of beer in the trains to the northern termini with them. _ _ _ .

11 hen darkness fell upon the streets of London thousands of wearers, of all ages, of the "Honesty and Liberty" button gave themselves up to liberty and licence. They swarmed through the West End and as far'east as Fleet-street, storming the public-houses on their way and .frequently bursting into cheers and snatches of comic songs. The scenes in Piccadilly bore a striking resemblance to Boat Race night; in the Strand a mild form of " mafficking " was indulged in. Places of amusement, such as animated picture shows and the "lightning travel" exhibitions, were open, and Villiers-street more particularly was as rowdy and vulgarly indecent as a common fair-ground at night. Horseplay and profanity were the outstanding features of this crowd.

Hardman ; yeast, Mr. Kershaw •, straw, Mr. Barlow ; crockery, Mr. Bailey ; horse and hearse hire, Mr. Connor ; plumbing requisites, Messrs. S. and P. Acton. The minutes were passed. PAINTING THE INFIRMARY. Five tenders for the painting of the outside of the Infirmary were submitted to the Board rid it was decided to ac 3ept that of Mr. Ellis P Clare, Forster- -street, Warrington, at £66 ss. ASSESSMENT COMM in E.E. A discussion arose r s to the filling of the vocrncy on , the Assessment Committee reused by the resignation of Mr. S. Davies. the Local Goverr tent Bo.frd having suggested that it should be proraeded with immediately. There were two propositions—that the vacancy should be filled at onca and that it should be deferred until after the election in Howley Ward. The voting was equal and the Chairmra gave bis casting vot ) in tavoor I of postponing the appointment N S.P.C.C. SUBSCRIPTION. The Board decided to anew its annual subreription of nve guineas to the funds of the N.S O.C.C. THE PAYMENT OF ARMY ANJ NAVY PENSIONS. A letter was read from the liatter. tg UP;OLI forward- ing the following resolution for endorsement by the • Board. It RJ9 requcated that copies be sent to the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for War and the First Lord of the Admiralty. P.-It this Botee, having in mind the atiangements t`,at a.: being made to pay old age r msions weakly at the Post Offices next year, earnestly trusts that the Governa ent will be able to arrange for the aiaay and r-.vy pensions to be paid weekly. The Board is anxious for this to be done for the following reasons.—(l) As an act of consideration to a class of pensioners for whom it thinks the Govern- ment must feel a peculiar responsibility, r 1 well ea an anxious regard for their welfare and dignity. (2) That these men have not teen accustomed to receive money in large sum:- and as a consequenr ) (with the aid of importunate comrades who will not let them alone) too often spend the whole of their quarters' allowance in dissipation within a week or fortnight after they have received same. (3) That to our knowledge many men who have been working steadily and giving satisfaction to their employs, have lost their employment in this way through absenting themselves from wort., and have ultimately become habitual tramps and a burden on the rates in one form or another. (4) That the system of paying these pensions quarterly is not only a waste of Imperial funds, but causes the ruin and degradation of many of our country's defenders who would otherwise be living comfortable and respectable lives and be a credit instead of a disgrace to the country." The CHAIRMAN: I take it you will adopt that. I would, with all my heart. The members were signifying assent, when Mr. JOLLEY remarked that it was not customary for the Board to comply with requests of that kind with- out fully understanding them. The CHAirrafael: I quite agree that it has not been the custom of this Board to fall in with a great many resolutions sent by other Boards, but I have often thought it was a great mistake that these pensioners were only paid once in three months. It actually happens that many go on the " booze " for eight or ten days and then there is nothing left for the remainder

of the time. I have always looked upon it that it has been a little bit too much trouble for the Government officials to pay the pensions weekly instead of quarterly. If there is any other reason I should be glad to hear it. The CLERK: The Boards of Guardians up and down the country have an Association known as the Poor Law Union Association an 1 all these matters are thrashed out there from time to time. I think it is of very little use for inlividual Boards to take this matter up. It is a question which has come before Boards of Guardians times without number in the past. If your wish to pass a resolution on the 'patter to-day I should recommend you to pass one to the effect that it be referred to the Poor Law Union Association. I The CHAIR MAN said that in face of the clerk's explanation he agreed that the resolution would have more -weight if it came from the Poor Law Unions Association. He moved that the question be referred to that organization. Mr. JOLLEY in seconding said he strongly dissented from the quiet assumption underlying the circular that the majority of Army and Navy pensioners were dis- reputable persons. Such an assumption was utterly unwarrantable. The great majority of the men were very deserving and worthy citizens and iu such few cases as ware indicated and the difficulties regarding which had led to action being taken wilh a view to the pensions being paid in weekly sums, could be met by the local Boards of Guardians if the members chose to take the trouble. It was not good enough to cast aspersions on a splendid body of men who had se: led their country faithfully. The resolution was agreed to. PENSIONS AND our RELIEF. I Mrs. WILKINSON gave notice that at the next meeting she would move :—" That all persons receiving relief from this Union and having no other di: paliftcation for the old age pension shall, after the first day of January, 1900, receive ss. per week for each single r3rson and 83. per week in the case of married couples."

div.head: " MERRIE ENGLAND."
div.p: " MERRIE ENGLAND."
MUSICAL SOCIETY'S FORTHCOMING OPERA.
Interviews with Mr. F. H. Crossley
and Mr. Foden Williams.

The music-loving public of Warrington is looking forward with a great deal of interest and pleasure to the performances of the opera " Merrie England" which will be given in the Royal Court Theatre by Members of the Warrington Musical Society from October 12th to 17th. We bear that the enterprise has been most enthusiastically taken up by all con- cerned, and there is every expectation that the opera company will add to their laurels by their presentation of this popular work which is,it should be remeeabered, entirely new to Warrington audiences. With the object of gleaning some information as to the musical 'promise of the opera, a representative of the " Eraminer " interviewed , Mr. Frank H. Crossley, the society's able and lindefatigable conductor, who has played a prominent I part in directing the forces engaged in the under- taking. He readily responded to the suggestion that Ihe should give some general impressions of the work lin hand. " Merrie England" he po;nted out is a purely romantic opera and the signal success of its ,• iuitial production at the Savoy Theatre in 1902 reminded I those present of the first nights of the most famous Gilbert ani Sullivan operas. The period selected, that lof Good Queen Bess, of Raleigh and of Essex, is the ' time associated in country life for some reason or I other with the May Queen and the Morris Dance. Mr. 'Crossley expressed the opinion that no composer could be chosen at the present time more fitted to n Ate the music in connection with such a period than Mr. Edward Garman who had already proved himself to be a past master in the art of writing old English dances.— As a matter of fact the leading idea of the opera is the dance. Mr. German has a peculiar gift for writing music and ear ecially dance music - Instinct with English idiom. His well-known" Three dances from Hemy VIII." have carried his name round the world. The score of " Merrie Englancl " continued Mr. Crossley, abundantly proves that on idward German the mantle of Sullivan has fallen. Particularly notable are the fine ensembles and the bri'liancy, delicacy and piquancy of the orchestration. His music, with the possible exception of the march played on the entrance of Queen Elizabeth,is quite free from the common-plc and is a credit alike to him and to the English school. In "Iferrie England" If r.German has given us his beat, and everybody knows how delightful this is. Capt .in Hood,the writer of the libretto, also seems to revel in the Elizabethian period. He has succee,d in making his Queen Elizabath, Raleigh and Essex a dignified trio, though they never seem at all out of place in the general scheme, the prevailing characteristics of which are lightness and delicacy. He has created in Walter Wilkins and Silas Simkins playeta in Shakespeare's company—a pair of diverting mummers whose fun is extremely amusing. Several of the numbers of the work, Mr. Crossley pointed out, will no doubt be received with special. admiration. • The quintet "Love is meant to make r 4 clad" is most charming in its daintiness end finish. There is a fine bre_ zy and manly ring in the setting of " Who are the 'Yeomen of England ?' and Elizabeth's solo "Oh peaceful England" with its stately rcinnet refrain and pianissimo ending is a beautiful number. Much humorous and clever music is contained in the Finale to Act 1, notably that associated with the Four Men of Windsor, but the funniest number in the whole opera is probably the "Fish Song," which is one of the cleverest things heard for many a day. There are also two charmings songs for Bessie Throckmorton, and a lovely duet for Jill all-alone and Raleigh. "It is the merry month of May" possesses quite Mendelssohnian.grace. _ _ .

Asked to indicate the outstanding features of the Musical Society'slortbcoming production of the work, Mr. Crossley said they had found " Merrie England" to be by far their largest operatic undertaking. It would he noticed that there was a very large cast and this, of course, enabled a greater number of membes of the society to take leading parts than ever before. Most of the principals are new people, which serves to demonstrate the resources of the society, in which c umection it is interesting to remark that most of the important pasts are "understudied." "And how do you anticipate the principals vrill acquit themselves.? ".as.the iron

4 I believe many of the new comets will score a great success and will, in fact, prove something of a revelation to the public." Mr. Crossley said the rehearsals had been very many and arduous the dancing alone, under litt. Foden skilful direction, hal,:ng occupied a great deal of time. As usual the society would have the valuable co-operation of its amat3ur orchestra, thereby being at a decided advantage as compare with many societies who had to pay heavily to obtain adequate professional orchestral help. The gratifying results so far obtained were entirely due to the sp!endid zeal and unselfish lovality of everyone concerned, the whole of the members of the chorus and orchestra vieing with the principals in their enthusiasm. "Then you anticipate the complete success of the forthcoming peyformances " "I believe that, barring accidents, we shall have a most successful week,—in fact " Jerrie England " should prove to be our best effort."

div.head: Chat With Mr. Peden Williams.
div.p: A Chat With Mr. Peden Williams.

The Warrington Musical Society's Opera Cmamittee has for a second year secured the services of Mr. Foden Williams as coach and stage manager, and lire short chat with one of our representatives he spoke in glowing terms of the prospects of the present enter- prise. The value of Mr. Foden Williams' good opinion is enhanced by the fact that he has had considerable experience in trair“ng amateur operatic societies in "Jerrie England," having produced the opera at Manchester (twice), Blackburn, York and Hull, a here in every case it has proved highly suer Nsful. Asked whether he anticipated an equally harpy consummation in Warrington, Ur. Foden Williams expressed his complete satisfaction with the work accomplished by tho opera company this season. " I do not thick ' he remarked "that we were ever in a I tter po4ition to be sanguine, and I anticipate the company will excel all theiroorevions efforts both from a musical and a histrionic paint of view." Mr. Foden Williams emphasised the fact that a sr 2cial feature of " Merrie England " is the dancing and he is inclined to think that the ability displayed by menbars of the musical s• ,:iety in this direction will c •asion not a little surpriz to thelr Watrington fiends. If the claimant happens to possess a copy of his birth certificate or other evidence of age he will, of course' produce it to the pension officer. It will be olr?rved that the arrange- ments refer only to evidence of births r.g:stered in England and Wales since Ist July, 1837. div.head: BRASS BAND CHAMPIONSHIP
div.p: BRASS BAND CHAMPIONSHIP
CROSFIELD'S BUD SECOND.

The national brass bind contest at the Crystal Palace on Saturday was a success from every point of view. The weather was a great factor in that success, for though some of the contests took place indoors, many of them had of necessity to be gone through in the open air. Not only were Londoners attracted to the Palace by the splendid musical treat, but it was a sight to them to see thousands of working men from the North rid West of England, with the difficult musics of Wagner's "Rienzi" In front of them carefully watching note by note and marking every little lapse. To many Londoners this was even more interesting than the music r3rformed by the bands themselves. The bands entered for the various competitions numbered 167, lent there were several absentees. Of the bands entered 33 hailed from Lancashire and Cheshire, a like number from Yorkshire, nearly el many from the Midland counties, and 26 from London. There was only one from Scotland, and the rest of England and Wales sent 41. But several of the Lancashire bands did not appear. With the thousand-guinea trophy was to be given a cash.prixe of £l9, together with instruments worth 28 gum • and medals which brought up the total to about £1,14g. The other prizes in this contest, of which there were six, ranged in value from £lO3 10s. to £l6. The non-appearance of Goodshaw, last year's runners-up for the championship, caused some dis- appointment, and Pemberton Old and Pendleton Old also failed to appear. This reduced the number of Lancashire bands in the champiorship section from 9 to ,6. The absence of Cleckheaton reduced the Yorkshire bands in the same section to three. The six Lancashire bands were Wingates Temperance (who won the trophy lest year and the year before), Shaw, Perfection Soap- works (Warrington), Gossage's Soapworka, Irwell Springs (a former champion) and Denton Original (also a former champion). The Yorkshire bands were Black Dike, King Cross Subscription, and Batley Old. Virtually It was a contest between Lancashire and Yorkshire. Before the judges announced their findings the general opinion seemed to be that there were five outstanding performances—those of Wingates, Black Dyke, Irwell Springs, Shaw, and Perfection Soapworks (Crosfiell's.) Obviously the judges could give no decision except by a close and detailed comparison of points awarded for the selection section by section. Meanwhile the evening's massed band concert pro- ceeded. The bands selected to take part in it were the Wingates Tompe.anoe, Batley Old, Bla ok Dike Mills, Denton Original, Goodshaw, Goeraage's Soap Works, Irwell Sprlags, Perfection Soap Works' and Rushden Temperance, but Goodshaw dropped out at the last moment. The Wingates Band gave its remarkable rendering of "Gems of Schumann, ' which so impressed the judges of the contest last year that they awarded the maximum number of marks to the performance. At the close the result was announced as follows,and it will be seen that though Wingatt failed to score a third successive victory the trophy again goes to Lancashire: Championship Section.-1, Irwel ••;pri ngs (conductor, Mr. W. Rimraer) ; 2, Perfection Soap Works, Warring- ton (Mr. W. Halliwell) 3, Wingates Temperance (Mr. W. Rimmer) ; 4. Shaw (111-. W. !Zimmer); .3,Black Dike Mills (Mr. W. Rimmar) ; 6, Luton Red Cross (Mr. A. Holden); 7, Kettering Rifles (Mr. A. Owen). - The many Warrington admirers a Crosfield's band had been earnestly hoping that they would win the championship, but it was recognized that they had a formidable task before them. While some little dis- appointment was felt that the band did not attain the premier position, there was general gratification at the fact that they had proved themselves worthy of ranking so high in the national competition. The ba9d returned to Warrington at 10.15 on Sunday night and had a cordial reception from a large crowd which assembled in the vicinity of the Bank Quay Station. They.at once proceeded to the works to the strains of one of their favourite marches and before dispersing played "Lead, kindly light." FIRST THREE BANDS VERY CLOSE. _ _

The London correspondent Of—tlie-7‘-ife—n-chester Guardian" writes :—lt was obvious even to the listener who bad not to make detailed criticism of the playing of the bands in the national contest at the Crystal Palace on Saturday that the first few hands are very close together, but I learo from the judges therrec'ves that it was a difficult matter to decide between the firbe, three—lrwell Springs yerfection,end Wingatn. There was a greater gap between the third band and the fourth. It is not certn'n whether the number of points awarded to each of the bands will be published this year, but there was no such gap this time as the forty points that separated Wingates from the second on the list last year. The success of the Festival at the Palm. 3 his led to the arrangement of a band contest at the Franco-British Exhibition on October 17th. Already about forty bands are entered for it, and after the contests, of which there will be four, carried on simultaneously in different parts of the grounds, there will be a massed band performance in the Stadium.

MY DEAR CEILDREN, Since I printed the stocies last week about animals, one of my readers, who used to live on the Solway Firth, and whom I met the other day a long way from that part of England, told me such a funny dog story, which .1 should like you all to hear. It was like this:— My little friend, who rejoiceein the name of i.,inie, had a brother, whose name was Jim, i...nd between them they yossessed a nice little Scotch'terricr, which was so full of fun, and got into such mischief, that at last Annie's lather said the dog 'must e got rid of, and they and throw the poor thing i to the Irish Sea. Of course, Jim and Annie were in a terrible state about the untimely end of their favotirite playmate, but their father could not be paci- fied, so the dreadful deed had to be done. The little dog was safely placed into a big basket, with a string round its neck, to which had been attached a heavy stone: This was safely carried right away to the iend of the Pier, but when they got to the end both of my little friends had an argument as to who should throw ,in the dog. Annie declared that she could not do it, and Jim likewise vowed that he was not equal to tho task. However, as they dare not go back without obeying orders, Annie finally turned her back upon the sea, while Jim shut his eyes and cast the poor animal into the briny ocean. Without stopping to watch the fate of their beloved terrier, they ran away up the pier as, hard as they could go, and made for home with sad hearts. Here comes the funny part of the story, for when they reached their own house, wondering how they would get on without their companion, the little dog sat on the doorstep wagging his tail. I am sure you will think it deserved to be kept after that, and it was. In spite of what some people say, this story is perfectly true, and I do not mind giving a nice box of chocolates to any member who can send me a better on.
Next week I hope to be able to tell you the result of our last Competition. Your affectionate, UNCLE NED.

• A. LITTLE JAPANESE. If pa been born across the seas, In a little house of clean bamboo, Among the flowering cherry-trees;—. If I'd been fed on fist-rand rice, The queerest nuts that ever grew, And all the different sorts of teas;— If I'd been used to a jiiariki-sha, And never seen a railroad car, Perhaps it wouldn't seem so nice TD be a Japanese! But "Mary Jane" does sound so plain, Compared. with " Neo Ina Yan"; And such a place as "Jones' Creek" (That's where I live and must remain) Could not be found in all Japan I Instead of "Pike's " or "Skinner's Peak," Of Fuji-yama there they speak— • The Sacred Mountain by the seas. Ho W elegant geographies Must be in Japanese! We have such very common things, Like pts in pens, and coops,of hens, Round corner-store that smell of cheese; While they have storks, with spreading wings, That live among the reedy fens. Their girls have paper parasols And painted fans, as well as dolls; They wade in flowers to their knees, And live a life of joyous ease, The happy Japanese. Yet mamma wouldn't be the same With heady eyes and, funny name, • And might not care so much for me. And—come to think—they never can Have any Christmas in Japan! They worship curiositiesi Great metal idols, made 4ity man About the time the world began. So, on the whole, I'd rather be A quiet little English girl Than a little Japanese.
RUNNING FOOTMEN. FOOTMEN.

In former days, whencoaches did not go above five miles an hour, and roads were not macadamised, footmen used to run before their masters. They were considered indispensable attendants upon the carriage of a great man, and doubtless their services were often in requisition. They cleared the way, paid the turnpikes, helped to pull the carriage out of the ruts or to support it on each side to prevent its being overturned; and they bore torches which in London they put out on their return home by means of the iron extinguishers attached to the lamp railings, such as maf yet be seen in front of the old houses in May Fair. The dress of the running footman was often gaudy, and he carried in hie hand a long pole, six or seven feet long, with a silver ball at the end, made hollow, whieh was to hold an egg or some wine. The pole was also used for leaping ditches or hard parts of the road; and great feats in-this way are recorded of some footmen. The powers of endurance of these men were wonderful. It is asserted that in a bad road they could easily keep ahead of a coach-and- six, but on level ground the pace of the horses would be somewhat slackened on their account. It was not unusual for them to go. sixty miles in the day.

BY A _ A well-known gentleman of Savannah tens this story: I notice in.this morning's paper an interesting account of hole a dog was made to testify in a ease in which he was claimed by a soldier who had at one time been in the English Army in India. According to the account, the soldier said that if the deg did not understand the Hindustani language he would not claim him, but if he did he would consider the dog belonged to him. When the case as called in court, the soldier said something in Vie Hindu tongue, and the deg -immediately recognised him, and, running through the crowd, jumped into the witness- box and fawned on the soldier." Another .said that this was a case similar to one which occurred in Savannah many years ago, before steamships went to that port. A gentleman owned a very valuable mocking bird, of which he thought a good deal.. The bird was stolen. The gentleman was vezy much put out over it, and hunted every- , where to recover it. He heard of a visitor from the North who had purchased a mock- ing-bird and was about to leave the port ort a sailing vessel. The gentleman concluded that he would go down to the vessel to see if the bird was not his. Upon reaching the vessel, sure enough; he found a man with a. mocking-bird which he at once recognised as the one which- he had lost. He told the visitor that the bird belonged to him, and the visitor asked how he could recognise the bird from any other, and was unwilling to give it up until some evidence had been given of ownership. The Savan.nahian finally said that he would make complfint before a magistrate, and if ,he did not prove it by the bird itself, he would not make any • further claim. So together they went before Magistrate Railford, who had his office at the time in a little building where the Custom-house now stands. The complaint was made, and the claimant of the bird said that he would prove that the mock- ing-bird was his, by the bird' itself. The magistrate was somewhat surprised, and asked: "How are you going to do that? The gentleman • replied that he would whistle an air, and if the bird took it up and followed him, it ought to be sufficient evidence of ownership. If the bird did not follow him, - then he would snake no further claim to it. He whistled the tune of "St. Patrick's Day in the Morning," and the bird joined in and whistled it through without interruption. The magistrate said: " I am satisfied that the bird is yours. I don't wish any further evidence of the fact of ownership,' The visitor was charmed, and wanted the bird badly, and offered £2O for it, but the owner refused to part with it for any amount.—" Savannah News."
OLD RHYMES IN NEW DRESS.

"There was a jolly miller lived on the river Del." A miller lived upon the river Dee. He was a jolly man, and all day long He worked and never stopped his cheery song: I wish with all my heart that we could see More people like him; blithe indeed was he, And comely, too, puissant, sturdy, strong, Loved by the people that he lived ,amoug. "I care for no one, no one cares for me," Was, it is true, the burden of his lay. But sung by him it meant not just the same That it would mean if it were sung some day, By some one else, perhaps. I think that we Should thus interpret the good miller's aim, "I care for all, and all do care for me."

" Simple Sinten went. a-fi.shing." A boy named Simon sojourned in a dale, . Some said that lie was simple, but I'm sure That he was nothing less than eimon pure; They thought him so because, forsooth, a whale He tried to catch in mother's water pail. litte boy, timid, composed, demure,— He had imagmation. Yet endure Defeat he could, for he, of course, did fail. But there are.Simons of a larger growth, Who, too, in shallow waters fish for whales, And when they fail they are "unfortunate." If the snail boy is simple, then are both, And the big Simon more, who often rails At what he calls ill luck or unkind fate.

" There was a man who had d cow, And'he had naught to give her." - A cer+ain, pper had a nice, fine cow, But rile same piper was a thriftless-man, He spent his substance feting the god Pan., And piped and, danced, but hever touched thil plow. , And when no hay nor corn was in the mow (The oove grown thin, and dim her coat of tan), He pulled his bagpipes out and then began To play the beast a tune. Her noble brow Grew dark; the piper in his blandest tone Then said, "Consider, cow, commune Pt, She always had been wont to ruminate, So she considered well, then with a moan Meekly replied, "I cannot eat your tune." Heroic ,cow, who had to stand and wait!

The term " Inland Correspondence " means -cor- respondence posted within the United ICingdom, including tha Isle of Manand the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence " is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent •by letter post, the only limitation. being that of size.

LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight Id. For every additional 2 0zi.... A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet imlength, one foot in width, or one foot in depth.

POST-CARDS. The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 31 inches in width, or be less than 3/ inches in length by 2} inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and finch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter.

HA.LFPENNY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 20z. in weight. Printed matter, &c., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. .

The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is J. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For a parcel ... ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 19 exceeding 1 lb. Pr 2 lb. 0 4 I 1 „ 21b. If 31b. 0 5 /9 „ lb. If 5 lb. 0 6 99 „ 5 lb. 91 7 lb. 0 7 If 9t • 7 lb. 97 8 lb. 0 8 1/9 99 Sib. 99 91b. 0 9 /9 II 9 lb. ft 10 lb. 0 10 10 lb. 11. lb. 0 11 No parcel may exceed 111 b. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel 13:— Greatest length... ... ... ... 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring Mt. 6in, in its longest dimensions as much as 21t. 61n. round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker; thus, if it measure no more than 31t. in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel" Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditiens similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. • The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. • MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only _cash them. at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional epart of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 61; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of rcdvice; a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORMIRS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order , may be issued for 'places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, 6d. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 6d. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphedio certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. _

These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by lid., from 6d. to El Is. The poundage fees are up to 2s. 6d.; Id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums.

- TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d. which covers 12 words, and an additional id. jot each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sons out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 ls. TELEGRAMS (kOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. PoST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.

_ .... These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the animal deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in sviiieh the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is lor over, a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 2i per cent. Any amount up to and including £l. may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presentin,, a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the d tie when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for perposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can bee xpeciited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELEPFIONE AND Treuxic LINS Crranous. . _ .

MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REGULATIONS. Each one must be registered with the council of a county or county borough, the fee being £1 fored motor oar, and 58. for a motor cycle. A register a number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep affixed when driving. Each driver must possess a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other effences. The highest speed at which a car rney be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1003), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dargerous to the publics, having regard to ell the circumstances of the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to be presence of the motor car on the road, the river must supply his name and address, and the tsvner and number of the car, under heavy penal- odie The driver must produce his licence at the sequest of a police constable.

div.head: Warrington's First Win.
div.p: Warrington's First Win.

Warrington gained their first win of the season on Saturday when they had Rochdale Hornets as visitors. There was a crowd of 5,000 and the improved display of the locals gave much satisfaction. W. H. Dowell, the Welsh International forward, made his first appearance for Warrington. The weather was bright and pleasant when the game opened, bet befora half-time a heavy rain storm came on and lasted throughout the game. Terms and officials: .

_ Warrington—Tilley, back; Fish, Dickinson, Cart- wright and Jordan, three-quarter backs; Brooks and denking, half-backs; Dowell, A. E. Boardman, P, Boardman, Naylor, Belton and Hewitt, forwards. Rochdale Hornets —Hollinrake, back; Hartley, Threl- fall, Robinson and Turner,three-quarter backs; Schofield, and Ledgard, half-backs; Richardson, Crabtree, Dearden, Walker, Thomas and Pearson, forwards. Referee Mr. W. McCutcheon (Oldham). Touch judges, Messrs. J. Edwards (St. Helens) and E. Pearson (Leigh). Warrington opened in very vigorous fashion, the forwards rushing the game to within a few yards of the line where Fish nearly got over. Then Cartwright got possession and WRS held up close in. The visiting full back finally cleared, but the Hornets could make little headway against the vigour of the home team. Lack of finish by. the home backs -caused several opportunities to be missed, Jordan once kicking too hard when he should have dribbled over. After about ,10 minutrfsplay Tilley opened the scoring with a clever dropped goal. War- rington now seemed to get into full stride and Fish scored a wonderful try after smart passing between Brooks, Jenkins and Dickenson. Soon after Jenkins gave Fish another opening with a neat crosskick, and the left winger again beat the opposition cleverly. Half-time ;—Warrington 1 goal 2 tries 8 points, Roch- dale nil. Turning round Rochdale showed ne splendidly, despite the fact that the game was played in a deluge of rain, Hartley scored RS the result of loose work by the Warrington backs, and after Brooks bad failed to break through, Cartwright crossed. A desperate forward rush led up to P. Boardman scoring, and in the last few minutes the Rochdale backs exhibited fine passing, and Tamer scored an unconverted try. Result :—Warring- ton 2 goal 4 tries (16 points), Rochdale Hornets 2 tries (6 points).

. RUNC9RN v. WIDNES. At Runcorn, befofe 3,000 spectators. The home forwards had the better of the opening play, and eventu- ally Padbury got possession,and ran to the Widnes line, where he handed to Jolley, who scored at the corner. Richardson failed at goal. On the resumption a fine round of passing by Flanagan, Rees and Padhury ended in the last-named scoring. Jolley failed with the goal kick. Runcorn continued the attack, and gave Widnes an anxious time but Jones defended well. Jolley got possession and dropped a goal from almost half-way, Just before the interval Deakin added another try, .which Jolley improved. Ha f-time score :—Runcorn Tgoals, 3 tries (13 points) ; Widnes, nil. ' After the interval rain fell in torrents, and left the ground in a sodden condition. Padbury was forced to retire injured. From a penalty kick Aspey placed a goal for Widaes, and after a smart' run Taylor dashed over; scoring a flue try, to which Aspey added a goal. The game was keenly contested in the closing stages, but without further score. Result :—Runcorn, 3 goals, 3 tries (13 points) ; Widnes, 2 goals, 1 try (7 points.) Teams : Runcorn—Harrison, back ; Deakin, Unsworth Hughes, and Flanagan, three-quarter backs; Jollev and Viratton, half backs; Walker, Padbury, Richardson, Rees, Dixon, and Langley, forwards. • Widnes—Jones, backs ; Barber, Lambert, Taylor, and Ditchfleld, three-quarter backs ; Hicks and Lally, half backs ; Aspey, Curtis, Rigby, Lynch, Morgan, and McCarthy, forwards. Referee, Mr. W. Nevins, Warrington. Touch judges, Messrs. T. A King, Salford, and T. Foulkes, St. Helens.

div.head: ' KANGAROOS."
div.p: THE ' KANGAROOS."
Australian professionals' Arrival.

• The Australian team of Rugby professional footballers who are to tour the constituency of the Northern Union arrived in London on Sunday. Passengers on board the P. ands°. liner Macedomn, the team disembarked at Tilbury Dock after having had a most pleasant voyage, and for the next four months they will be busily engaged playing the matches at the rate of two a week. The tourists on their arrival at Tilbury. were met by deputation from the Northern Union, consisting of Messrs. J. Nicholl (Halifax), .1. B. Cooke (Wakefield), H. Ashton (Warrington), J. W. Wood (Leeds), W. 1). Lyod (Hull), J. H. Smith (Widnes) and J. Platt (Oldham). Mr. J. J. Giltinan, the manager of the team who had travelled overland from Marseilles, was also one of the party waiting for the arrival of the foot- ballers. The parties on board and those on the dock side exchanged greetings in good time, and almost before the Macedonia had come alongside, the footballers ranged thernsalves on deck and startled the ship's company with their war cry, delivered with full throated vigour and business-like gt stures. A war cry is now, of course, a necessary part of the itinerary of every touring Colonial team, but the declamatory aboriginal passages which the Australian professionals have adopted as their challenge to the world form a cry of weird and awful effects. But the" Kangaroos" —for that is the name by which they will be known— have gone further than that, and they have acquired a mascot in the shape of a live silver-grey kangaroo, which, it is intended, shall be on view at every match which the tourists play. The kangaroo ,as not in evidence yesterday—it will not, indeed, arrive until later in tho week—but the war cry was not sufficiently theatrical to draw attention to a body of men who apparently had been general favourities on board the ship which brought them from Australia.

The Australians took a fine body of men—sturdy,' clean-limbed, and well proportioned, though, as a body, they may not have quite the height or the weight of the All Blacks.
