div.head: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
By . Veronica.
AN INTERESTING RECORD.

I hear that Mr. W. Ethelbert Henry, C.E., who has r been conducting the "Answers to Correspondents" columns of " The Amateur Photographer," since January, 1893, is relinquishing that work, Probably few readers have any idea of the amount of research and varied knowledge that is required for such a post. Not , only must the man be an excellent technician, but he I must have a very fine reference memory, and also a good I reference library and a good system of preserving arc!' arranging cuttings, for he is obliged to keep his refer- ence collection absolutely up to date. In addition to, this, he must be well in touch with experts in the different branches of photography, so that his own knowledge may be supplemented by reference to their stores of (often unpublished) experience. In conduct- ing the A.P. column for nearly thirteen years, Mr. Henry has supplied nearly 700 contributions, of which i each is equal n actual writing to a lengthy article. During this time he has dealt with not less than 4,700 different subjects, and probably the total is quite twice or three times this number. PICTORIAL WORN AT THE R.P.S. EXHIBITION. ' I wrote last week of the professional, and some other sections, of this very great and very interesting exhibition, and devote this week's notes to the pictorial section in the hope that many of my readers may be able to visit the great show and to consider for them- selves the justice or otherwise of my remarks. It has always been considered that the Photographic Salon dealt solely or mainly with extremely advanced work, much of which was experimental, even to the verge of rashness or audacity, while the R.P.S. dealt with the sound sober "Middle-class" photography which was not likely to startle anyone. During the last few years,the R.P.S. exhibition has been advancing until it was capable of inoluding anything that would be acceptable at the Salon, while it retained enough of the older style of work to prove its catholic outlook and to make some attempt to satisfy all classes.

div.head: ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE • TWO EXHIBITIONS.'
div.p: ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE • TWO EXHIBITIONS.'

It is difficult to define what are exactly the relative outlooks of the two selecting committees, but one may ,v?ughly say that the Salon looks for some definite pictorial intention, some " message" of a poetic or imaginative character, while the Royal looks for sound technique, considering that word in ii wide enough sense to include such matters as composition, light and shade, tone-rendering, etc., and not merely as dealing with the technical methods of negative and print- making.

div.head: DISTINCT DISAPPOINTMENT.
div.p: A DISTINCT DISAPPOINTMENT.

The pictorial section of the R.P.S. this year is a great disappointment to me, for I think that it marks a serious drop from the high-water level of last year and the year before. There is an enormous amount of good sound interesting work, but there is also a large proportion (at least one-third of the whole collection) of pictures which ought not to be accepted now-a-days by a first-class exhibition. Noting the great number of people who have one or two prints, I incline to the idea that the selecting committee was swayed by a generous kind-hearted wish to represent every man who had submitted pictures if by any possibility this could be done.

div.head: CHIEF FAULTS.
div.p: THE CHIEF FAULTS.

Of course, in an exhibition like this, even in its worst examples ,shows only faults that are common to a great deal of photography, and which, by their very familarity have come to be disregarded by most photographers. It Is for the sake of awaking photographers to a sense of the greater possibilities that critics write their ' essays, and it is very disheartening when one finds that after years spent by many able writers in hammering away at certain very definite and very palpable blemishes in the work, these same faults are almost as common as ever. Tone-rendering has been the subject of many a sermon, and many an illustration in photographic journals, yet a large proportion of the pictures found in such an exhibition as the Royal are woefully out of tone. We do not see so many of the bald-headed skies as we did some time ago though many landscape workers have not yet realised that the mere printing in of any sort of cloud is not sufficient to bring a landscape and sky in tone. A common fault in to-day lies in including great masses which are as black as the process will allow, which have no detail and gradation, and which represents nothing that has ever been seen in nature in conjunction with the detail and gradation that one finds in the half-tones and highlights of the same pictures. Most of these masses are due to simple ignorance, and to under-exposure. In some cases, however, they are introduced purposely with a view to giving etrength of contrast. They require the careful consideration of every picture-maker.

div.head: HARD FACTUAL TREATMENT.
div.p: HARD FACTUAL TREATMENT.

Few photographers seem to realise that when one looks at a scene in nature one does not find much of harsh sharp-cut outline and contrast, but that every- thing appears soft-edged, and the tones and colours blend into one one another harmoniously, except when one focusses the eyes consciously upon some small piece of detail such as a leaf or the edge of a branch. In nature, there is always a feeling of roundness, distance and space, but the tendency of the photographic lens and plate tespecially when the latter is not ortho- chromatic) is to emphasise sharp outlines and edges. Fuzziness has been ridiculed and condemned, and a great deal of the ignorant work which has been done in the effort, to obtain " broad " effects is only fit for condemnation. On the other hand, one will seldom get any satisfactory effect of atmosphere and light while one keeps to the crisp harsh methods of ordinary photography. A very good example of the softer and more truthful treatment is to be found in the half dozen figure studies shown at the R.P.S. by M. GE Boon, and the same sort of thing has been well exemplified for many years past in the work of Percy Lewis, W. T. Greatbatch, Alexander Keighley, Arthur Marshall and others. Without asking my readers to do so far as Mr. Marshall has done in his more extreme work, I suggest that those who remember the general landscape of the four photographers above mentioned and who will use that memory as a guide for testing the treatment of the landscwes in the present exhibi- tion will learn much as to which are good and which are less good, in this direction at any rate.

div.head: Brewers' Picnic.
div.p: The Brewers' Picnic.

--- Sir,—ln last Sunday's picnic to London we have the old proverb startlingly illustrated that "Satan ffnds some mischief still for idle hands to do." When the plutocrary and the raobocrary are in alliance you may be sure that mischief is brewing and that noise and threatrical effect and not argument is the order of the day. We are told that 250,00 were there and being there what did they demonstrate? Certainly not that the country was against the Licensing Bill. Oh dear, No! A great many were there because of a cheap outing and would have gone anywhere on the cheap; great many more were there because they were engaged in making or selling the stuff and were therefore not free agents but were bound to toe the line at the behests of their employers. When you have eliminated these two 1 sections of the great picnic how many of the free and independent electors of Britain are left? Yet even many of these ci:d not attend so much to oppose the Licensing Bill as to show their dislike to the present Government because it happened not to be of the same political complexion as themselves. The demonstration was a sham from beginning to end and simply engendered by the funds of the great brewery trusts which the men of England in the near future will have to contend against if they would keep their national beverage pure and wholesome. Seeing that the Established clergy in Warrington supported the Trade some time ago I would like to ask them if they approve of the desecration of the Sabbath for such an object as that of last Sunday ? Surely the Trade ought to be quite competent to get up a demonstration on some other day.—l remain, yours &c.. PUIL SQUOD.

div.head: Beer as "The Last Hope."
div.p: Beer as "The Last Hope."

Sir,—The Brewers' fraternity are putting forth every effort to try and convince the English elector -that black is white and rice versa,. Unfortunately the elector is led away on occasions. It is rather a pity he does not reason more within himself, then he would not be duped so easily. The prospect of an extra pint must have upset the equilibrium of the average Novocastrian. Newcastle seems to have shifted its centre of gravity from coal to beer—glorious beer—otherwise the " last hope." A friend of mine in the Midlands, who seems to be a bit of a poet, has forwarded me the following lines.— Yours Latchford. The Brewers show our" blunders," They promise to do wonders, And make some think that no one else can guide;
H. F.

But to. me its rather funny That they with all their money Should quite ignore the problem—Unemployed. The Tories they keep spouting Yes—you even hear them shouting— If they could but get the masses on their side ; Both millionaire and miser, With Bill and his Eliza, And all the dupes, then you would be employed. The suffragettes are terrors, They think they don't make errors : And mean to have their way from either side. You marry one—you'll know it ; When vexed you dare not show it ; "Votes for Women" snuff you'll get when unemployed.

You're neither rogue nor scamp, Though you've had to do the tramp. As you had'ut got the money for to ride ; You've tramped the country o'er Till your feet were aching sore And not allowed to beg, though Unemployed. Yet the Ballot is your power Do you never think one hour Only on the football news or racing guide ; At the polling you're not ready. You act like "Come up, Neddy " That's all you know about tho unemployed. They say the "Lords" are needless Some "Commons" are as heedless, It's the simple-headed voter has to guide— You never read a word All you know is what you've heard; That's why we have so many Unemployed. I always take a pleasure In supporting a good measure Independent of party, creed, or side; One thing I'd like to mention, That is the Old Age Pension, As it helps that class that canot be employed.

div.head: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. --- Wesleyan Trustees' Appeal.
div.p: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. --- Wesleyan Trustees' Appeal.

The monthly meeting of the Warringion Union Assessment Committee was held at the Workhouse yesterday, Mr. J. Billing° presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. A. J. Jolley, G. Mather, A. Brooks, W. Gill, J. Evans, W. Furness, A. Bottomley (clerk), R. R. Meacock (valuer), W. H. Woodcock (assistant over- seer for Warrington), and Joseph Smith (assistant overseer for Great Sankey). WESLEYAN TICETEES' APPEAL. Alderman Ei.LP,ON appealed on behalf of the trustees of the Latchford Wesleyan Church against the assess- ment of the two cottages' 2 and I,Thelwall-lane,at £lO 10s. gross and LC) ratable. He stated that the two dwell- ings had been made into one and the building was let to the caretaker of the church who paid the trustees ss. per week rent. Mr. WooDcocx said the overseers were of the opinion ' that the premises were correctly assessed. They were worth ss. Gd. per week. The CHAIRMAN said the overseers evidently con- sidered it was an equitable assessment and considering that the Wesleyans of Latchford were wealthy he pre- sumed they would not differ from the opinion of the overseers. (Laughter). Alderman ELLISON : We do not consider that we are wealthy and that is why we appeal for a reduction. The Committee declined to make any change in the assessment.

THE ASSESSMENT OF A EAR:q. Mr. BAXTER BENNETT appealed against the assess- ment of the Grange Farm, Great Sankey, which stood as follows :—Farmhouse and buildings, gross £27, ratable .£23 land. gross £192 10s., ratable £lB3 • farm buildity, in hood-lane, gross £3, ratable £5. He con- tended that the whole of the farm was over-assessed, and particularly the land. He did not make much use of the building in Hood-lane. Part of the land was very rough and he did not get two pennyworth of stuff from some of it this year or last. Ihe rent of the farm MS £230 10s. Mr. JOSEPH Smira said the total increase of the assessment was £2l 10s. ratable.

The matter was referred to the valuer. WARRINGTON'S RATABLE VALUE. Mr. WOODCOCK submitted the new valuation list for Warrington which showed an increase for the half-year of .£2,060 10s. on the gross and .£1,657 10s. on the ratable value. Tha total valuation now stood; gross £311,811 10s, ; ratable .£23),017.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGE SCHEME. Threatened Abandonment.
div.p: THE SANKEY BRIDGE SCHEME. Threatened Abandonment.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee on September 23th, the Town Clerk read the following letter he had received from the County Bridgemaster : County Offices, Preston, 15th September, 1903. Sankey Canal Bridge. Dear Sir,—l have conferred with ray Chairman upon your letter of the lith instant, and have to express our very great regret that the action of your Council in definitely etating that they will give no financial assistance to a schema which is manifestly for the benefit of both the County and the Borough, leaves us no alternative but to abandon the proposed improvement. Yours faithfully, W. COMPTON BALL, County Bridgemaster. The Committee resolved that the County. Council be written to, urging the necessity of the improvement being proceeded with, and that the matter be referred to the following sub-committee, with power to wait upon the County Council if necessary :—Aldermen Bolton, Bennett, Tinnion, Councillors Evans, Wilkinson and Pemberton.

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB.
BOWLING PRIZES DISTRIBUTED. Mr. A. H. GrosiiiiK M.P., and the Unemployed Problem.

The Liberal Club presented a bright and attractive appearance on Thursday evening when the animal , distribution of prizes took place. A variety of plants and tloWers had been very tastefully arranged by the manager (Mr. Randall) and the effect was most pleasing. The presence of Mr. A. H. Crosfield, and Mrs. Crosfield lent great interest to the proceed- ings and they received a very hearty greeting from a lae,ge assembly which included a good muster of the fair sex. Mr. E. A. Sanders had arranged a capital musical programme and every item met with full appreciation. Miss F. Brown sweetly sang the waltz song from the opera "Tom Jones" and "Cumin' thro' the Rye." Mrs. E. A. Sanders delighted the assembly with her expressive interpretations of "Annie Laurie" and Tosti's "Good-bye," ' and Mr. A. Greenough sang "Take a pair of sparkling eyes " with success. Mr. A. Hale trave an acceptable rendering of " Lighterman Miss Gladys Hale supplying the pianoforte accom- paniment. A quartette party consisting of Messrs. R. W. Cook, W. Critchley, D. Gittens and W. Woodcock acquitted themselves with credit in that popular composition " Mary." Mr. E. Barnforth played a couple of 'cello solos with taste and skill. One of the most interesting features of the programme was a brilliantly executed pianoforte solo by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, which was enthusiastically received. The humorous element was sustained by Mr. E. A. Sanders who created great mirth by his recital " The Dinglebury Testimonial." Mr. George Anderton was an efficient accompanist. THE PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

During an interval, the i distri ut7on o prizes took • '1;-- - *- place. Mr. J. Worrall presided and was supported by Aldermen Pierpoint and Tinnion, Councillors Lockor, Dickenson and Wilkinson, Messrs. C. E. Parker, John Upson, T. Pemberton, W. Bibbv, P.Peacock, E.England, J. Critchley, T. Critchley, J. Howes, jun., and others. The principal award was the handsome silver cup presented by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield and of which the first holder is Mr. M. Tobin who, in addition to this trophy, received a medal. Mr. H. Daintith, who was second in the competition, was also the recipient of a medal. The prizes in the annual handicap, generously presented by Mr. A. H. Crostield, M.P., were won by the following :-1, F. Dale ; 2, A. Lawton ' • 3, G. Baster ; 1, H. Cook ; 5, H. Daintitla ; 6, F. Morrell ; 7, W. Warburton ; 8, J. H. Dutton •, .9, F. Plumpton ; 10, J. Critchley ' • 11, G. Vernon ; 12, T. Cooper ; 13, T. Shaw; 11. W. IL Dutton, jun.; 15, J. Gibson; 16, R. Marrow. Mrs. A. H. Cros field gracefully distributed the prizes. THANKING MR. AND MRS. CROSFIELD, THE POLITICAL SITUATION.

Alderman PIERPOINT, who was introduced by the Chairman as a stalwart of the Liberal party whom they were delighted to welcome, was warmly cheered on rising to propose a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield for their presence and generosity, Ile said he was afraid the warmth of their reception was greater than he deserved or expected, because unfor- tunately, although he might well be described as a stalwart of the Liberal party in Warrington, he thought if the Chairman had used the prefix " aged " it would have fittingly applied to him. He had been in that room under very different circumstances from those which brought them there that night. He had been there in periods of joy and in periods almost amounting to distress, to him at least. At that time he was surrounded by a body of men whom he knew intimately and many of whom had now joined the great majority. Failing powers precluded the possi- bility of his renewing the active part which he took with reference to Liberalism in the past, in fact it was impossible, because when one was getting near seventy years of age he thought it was quite time one was allowed to take that rest which he felt from a political point of view he was well entitled to ask for. They could, however, rest assured that his interest in Liberalism in Warrington had never slackened and never would. (Applause.) He had stuck to it in its days of progress and in its days of triumph. He stuck to it through the dark days which they had gone through, always doing the best he could to hold and maintain aloft the standard of Liberalism which, after all, from his own selfish point of view was best in his interests, and he thought they would all agree was best in the interests of this great country. (Applause.) The proceedings that night, continued the alderman, were better than a meeting at Hyde Park against the Licensing Bill. He thought the money had been well expended—that in Hyde Park was literally thrown away—at any rate he hoped so. This poor, unfortunate Liberal Government was said to be like a jelly fish, but he was bound to say that all the measures they had pro- posed had met with his sincere approval and he would accord them all the support he was able to give. (Applause). Was there anything that the Liberal Government of to-day had done that they would like to have remained undone ? Would they rather have a Conservative Government who would give them tariff reform instead of a Licensing Amendment Act? ("No.") He said : "Give me an amendment of the licensing law and let tariff reform be sent back to Birmingham, for them to take care of it there." (Applause). Referring to the presence of Mrs. Crosfield, Alderman Pierpoint said he was sure his friend Mr. Crosfield had made a wise and beautiful choice— a choice which he hoped would be with him for many years to come in order to make his life pleasanter as a married man than it was as a single man. (Applause.) As for their member, he (Alderman Pierpoint) was delighted with him. He thought he was doing his work as the representative of this great commercial borough in a manner which redounded very much to his credit. He (Alderman Pierpoint) believed he was right in saying that every Liberal elector of Warrington thought more ofiMr.Crosfield to-day than he did on the day when he obtained that magnificent majority. ( Applause.) He believed as the years went on—and he hoped a few more years would elapse before they had occasion to fight again—Mr. Crosfield would be able to show their Conservative friends that the confidence which the people of Warrington reposed in him at the last election would be more than quadrupled at the next. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN UPON, in seconding, said they cught not enly to thank Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield for what they had done that night, but also to congratulate Mr. Crosfield upon being a member of a party and a supporter of a Government which had done so much to redeem its election pledges—(hear, hear)—and to justify the con- fidence they placed in ill.. Crosfield and the party when they elected him some two years ago. In his (Mr. Upson's) reading of the political history of this country he noticed a remarkable fact—that when the other side was in power all eyes seemed to be turned outward, and when the Liberal party was in power all eyes seemed to be turned inward ; in other, words, when we had a Con- servative Government we had what was called a spirited foreign policy, aggressive diplomacy, provocative treat- ment of smaller nationalities, large expenditure on armies and navies, and entire forgetfulness of the need of ameliorative work for the great masses of this country. (Hear, hear.) By pursi.ing an attempt, at any rate, to put into practice the golden rule ininter- national relationships' the Liberal party was enabled not only to promote but to preserve peace, and also to give attention to the social injustices and economic wrongs which were still the disgrace of our modern life. (Applause.) It had been said that the Liberal party stuck to office and yielded to pressure, that it was nebulous and jelly fish in its nature and composition. He thought the legislative achievements of the Govern- ment had proved exactly the opposite. (Hear, hear.) Had they been desirous only of remaining in office, surely they would not have touched, as they had done, the great vested interests of this country. They would never have ir.terfered with "the trade." They woul:. not venture, as he hoped they shortly would,to touch that I still greater vested interest—the interest inland. (Hear, I hear). If the Liberal Government had wanted to remain in I office for office sake they would have let severely alone both the liquor trade and the question of the land. Many of them, continued Mr.Upson, thought that along the lines of national treatment of the land lay the great remedy for unemployment—(hear, hear)—and they believed that the force of the Government was not yet spent and that this greatest of all problems would be tackled by them in a masterful manner, so that the problems which so perplexed us to-day with regard to unemployment would be to some extent solved. (Applause). The work which the Liberal Government had done with respect to Old Age Pensions merited the heartfelt approval of all the men and women of this country. (Applause). It seemed to him that if there was such a thing as gratitude in politics—and there was uot—(laughter)—the mere passing of that Act would have kept the Liberal party in power fur this generation. He had referred to the courage with which they had touched the vested interests. When one thought of the immense power of those interests, the immense power of money behind them, the strenuous way in which those interests were fighting for what they considered their rights as against the common weal, when one remembered how great and bitter were the forces arrayed against the Government, one was almost inclined to give expression to the wail of the poet Lowell when he said that "Truth is ever on the scaffold Blight is ever on the throne." The teaching of history and their own faith taught them that the poet's conclusion was right, that after all the scaffold ruled the future and that "Behind the dim unknown Standeth God within the shadow Keeping watch above His Own." They could, therefore, take courage and with renewed energy and strenuous faith go on regardless of whether they lost Newcastles and Pec khams—( laughter)—regard- less of the fact that by-elections might go against them, only recognizing that they would do and support what was right. (Appjause). The vote was carried with enthusiasm.

The question of the Mayoralty for the coming year was considered at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee on Monday afternoon. After some dis- cussion a deputation consisting of Alderman Pierpoint and Bennett and Councillor Toole was appointed to wait upon Alderman Smethurst, asking him to accept office for another year. His decision will be announced at a special meeting of the committee, to be held on fuesday evening, shortly before the monthly meeting of the Council. Monday's meeting of the Committee was presided over by Alderman Forshaw, whose name has been freely mentioned in connection with the Mayoralty, in the event of Alderman Smethurst not continuing in office.

The final prize competitions of the 1908 season were held at the club range on Thursday, 24th September„ and Saturday, 26th September, when a total of 80 ' entries. in the various competitions, was reached. The ; weather on the Thursday was fine, but the light (which , at the best was not very good) soon failed, and shoot- ' ing then became a matter of difficulty, the scores being correspondingly low. On Saturday the light was very good, but operations were impeded by several heavy showers, which drew the competitors to shelter. In spite of these difficulties, however, no lack of enthusiasm was apparent, and some very good scoring was made. IThe principal event was the Service Rise Competition for the Donegall Bronze Badge, which is provided, annually, by the National Rifle Association, the winner being entitled to enter for the Donegall Cup and money prizes at every succeeding annual Bisley Meeting. Next in importance came the Miniature Rifle Competi- tion for the club medal. Eight other prizes were provided by the club for competition, and throe special prizes were kindly given by a member of the committee. The distance in all competitions was 100 yards, and Bisley conditions were observed. In the Donegall Badge Competition, a handicap of 10 per cent was imposed upon members of the Army and Territorial Force, and a handicap of five per cent upon ex-Army men and ex-Territorials, to compensate for the disadvantage under 'which civilian members of the club laboured when competing with men trained to the use of the service rifle. All other competitions were shot upon even terms. DONT:GALL BRONZE BADGE. (Service Rifle,)—This was won by Colour-Sergeant James Allardice, with a gross score of 50 points out of a possible 56, and a net score (after deducting handicap) of 44 points. It is worthy of mention that this is the second time, in succession, that Colour-Sergeant Allardice has carried ofl;the badge. The next highest score (38 points) was made by Mr. J. E. Hobin, but as he was subject to the 5 per cent, handicap above-mentioned, the second prize fell to Mr. A. Down, with a score of 37. The conditions in this competition were, 7. shots, 3in. bull's-eye and 7 shots, disappearing figure. The following scores were made :—J Allardice, 50; J E Hobin, 33 ; A Down, 37 ; W Plinston, 36 ; TI Fletcher, 35; A Warburton, 31; M Cowley, 31 ; H Owen, 29; F C Bennion, 29 ; F Garside, 28. CLUB MEDAL (Miniature Rifle).—The Club Medal was won by Mr. P. D. Gardiner, with a score of 51 out of a possible 56 points, the conditions being similar to the Donegan Bale. Scores :—P. D. Gardiner (Medal) 51; T Daintith second prize), 50 ; A Warburton, 46 ; C P Day, 44; J Robin 42; F M Cowley, 40 ;G H Ingram (Sergeant-Major), 39 ; A E Longshaw, 35 ; I Broady, 32; J Allardice (Colour-Sergeant), 30 ; R Thompson, 27. Ithem of the old towns. In that little experiment which they in Warrington were trying, they should bear in mind that they were really engaging in a very great work. because they were starting in Warrington —an important old town—a movement which was destined, if wisely carried out to effect marvellous changes for good in their midst. He confessed that when he was asked to take part in that ceremony he was anxious to see from the plans of their suburb scheme whether in laying it out they had due regard for the town as a whole. (Hear, hear.) He thought in the plans they had adopted they had already shown that regard and if he might make a suggestion he would urge them in erecting the houses to provide for any developments which might be required in the way of widening the main road. The promoters had very wisely made provision for open spaces in the suburbs. He would ask them to consider whether it would be wise of them to endeavour to get those spaces taken over by the local authorities and allow them to be used by the inhabitants at large. In that way some expendi- -1 tare would he spared to their undertaking, and at the I same time the community of Warrington generally would share in the benefits. Another point which was emphasised in Mr. Nettlefold's book on " Practical Housing" was the cost of roads. Mr. Nettlefold had a very wise method of dealing with the housing problem and he suggested that in garden suburb schemes they might adopt arrangements which would reduce the heavy cost of road-making, not by reducing the space between the houses but by reduaing the actual amount of road which was to be metalled, and providing borders of green sward on either side. As to the financial side of the scheme, there was a tendency in many minds to think that the limitation of the dividend was going to work in some way to the harm of the investors. He believed, however, that it was just the contrary because it tended to make the security of the investment much better than it would be if there were an attempt to ensure a large dividend. Further in projects of that kind, where they were working for the future, they were on much safer ground if they insisted on such requirements as to buildings and open spaces as would ensure the permanence of the invest- ment. If they observed the way in which building estates were often developed, they would quite see that under the twentieth century pinre some of those estates and the buildings upon them would have to be dealt with in a very summary way and the investors in such undertakings ran a risk which did not appertain to those who put their money in schemes which were carried out with an eye to the public well-being. They had a permanence in value which could never be secured by that class of invest- ment which sought to obtain great financial rewards for itself at a disregard of the health and comfort of the people. (Applause.) A movement of that kind must be of very great value to the people of Warrington. It would have the effect of reducing the death rate, which was at present high, because it had been found that the duration of life on such estates was longer than it was under ordinary conditions. Therefore those who sub- scribed to undertakings like that, though they might only get 5 per cent, on their money, would gain directly in health, even if they did not live on the estate,becarise such were the laws of the universe that our health was seriously affected by the health of those who lived near to us. He trusted the inauguration of that suburb would be the beginning of a great change in Warring- ton ; and that those who owned land contiguous to the estate would recognize some share in the responsibility and try to live up to their neighbour or oven to go one better, He trusted that the movement would add enormously to the prosperity of the old town of arrington. (Applause). Mr. A. H. Crosileld, M.P.,said it was his very pleasant duty and privilege to propose a double vote of thanks to Lady Greenall and Mr. Ebenezer Howard. In the first place he would like cordially to associate himself with what his friend Mr. Parker had said about Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall. He had long been familiar— he hardly liked to say over how many years his recollec- tions extended—(laughter)—with the great energy and activity of his old friend Sir Gilbert Greenall, and he was sure he was only expressing the opinion of all present when he said that ever since Lady Greenall came to live amongst them, there had been the same general admiration felt throughout the town for her great energy and active interest which had been shown in everything that was really for the benefit of Warring- ton. (Applause.) That was why they thought it was so very fitting that her ladyship had gracefully per- formed the ceremony of laying the foundation stone of ' that garden suburb. It had been extremely interesting to listen to the addresses from Mr. Howard and Mr. Parker. (Hear, hear.) They would all agree that it was very good of Mr. Howard to come down to War- rington, and his presence had added greatly to the interest of the proceedings, because they recognized in him the pioneer of a movement which, without exaggeration, they could not but . regard as a great movement in the present and a movement with still greater possibilities, many of which they hoped to see realized an the neighbourhood of Warrington. (Hear, hear). He thought the authorities who had taken the most active part in bringing the undertaking to its present stage were to be congratulated on the very charming site which had been secured. Personally he thought a pretty outlook from a house or a cottage I was always half the battle—(hear, hear)—and he was sure that in its pleasant surroundings main its accessi- bility to the industrial centre so close at hand, the neighbourhood should recommend itself very greatly indeed to many of the workpeople of Warrington. Mr. W. P. Rylands seconded and said they could perhaps appreciate the objects and ideals of the suburbs companies better when they passed along some of the streets of Warrington which perhaps were not much better than slums and thought what they would have been like had those who were responsible for their con- struction been actuated by the motives and desires which animated the garden suburbs promoters to-day. The vote was heartily carried and in responding Sir Gilbert Greenall expressed the hope that the develop- ment of the movement would b 3 of the greatest benefit to the working-classes of the town. A vote of thanks to Mr. Parker for presiding was proposed by the Mayor, who said he hoped that in a short time the Corporation would be able to cater for the convenience of the residents in the suburb by extending the tramway service. Canon Stevenson seconded and paid a tribute to the great business ability, marvellous energy aria pecuniary assistance which Mr. Parker had devoted to the work. Alderman Bennett in supporting said that in addition to the four houses now about to be erected, plans had been prepared for four more dwellings at Great Sankey and four at Grappenhall. The vote was heartily passed. At the close of the ceremony light refreshments were served in Sankey Church Sunday School. 'LECTURE AT THE TOWN HALL.

In the evening Mr. Ebenezer Howard delivered a lecture in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on the progress of the Garden City movement. The Mayor ( Uderman Smethurst) presided over a large attendance and spoke very hopefully of the prospects of the movement in Warrington, which had - his entire sympathy. Mr. Howard's lecture proved highly interesting, and dealt most exhaustively with the Garden City at Letchworth. which is proving such a gratifying success. He showed how the work could be applied to places like Warring- ton, in the building of suburbs. Numerous lantern slides were exhibited, the views of Bourneville, of which the lecturer spoke in very high terms, being particularly fine. The audience showed great interest in slides depicting the plans of the Warrington Garden suburbs and a sketch of the first four houses, the corner stones of which had been laid that day. Mr. Howard was warmly thanked for his lecture, on the proposition of Mr. E. E. PARKER, seconded by the Rev. Canon STEVENSON. The Mayor was thanked for his sympathy with the movement and for lending the Council Chamber on the motion of the Rev. C. HARVEY COOK, seconded by Mrs. B. ninu.tri, a member of the committee of the tenant association.

End of the Season.—Final Competitions.
PALACE AND HIPPODROME,

Kurkamp, the singing conductor, makes a popular return visit to the Palace and Hippodrome this week. He conducts the orchestra from a little platform in their midst and with his back to the stage, at the same time singing a couple of songs in a robust and pleasing tenor voice. A fine reception is accorded to II 0. Wills, the " Water Rat," a comedian of undoubted parts and ability. His songs have been enthusiasti- cally encored, and one effort in response was a recitation about "The child who was killed on the line." Even this was funny—except for the child, of course. The xylophone is an instrument which seems specially adapted for music-hall turns, and its various exponents are usually well received. This week the five Vernons from the London Empire appear as performers on an instrument which has to be hit hard and often. I, Their playing was often brilliant in the extreme, and brought down the house. The Gregson trio produce a side-splitting sketch entitled " The Dummy," in which a mistress, a maid and a page all play uncommon parts. A clever pair of dancers are Burns and Bentley, while the Sisters Cora take up a somewhat similar line as duettists and dancers and meet with success every time. Harry Milton is a Dutch comedian with a true sense of humour and a pair. of feet which also know something of dancing. The twin Sisters Edwards combine singing, dancing, and kettle-drum playing very effectively. The biograph, as usual, has some capital pictures, and Mr. Widdop's orchestra plays with a tastefulness which is generally admired.

Mr. A.lfred Sutro's famous play has been making its second appearance in Warrington this week, and large audiences have testified t) the popularity which " The Walls of Jericho " has earned all over the country. We doubt whether there is a stronger or more enthralling play running to-day, whirla the brilliance of the dialogue alone is suffiaient to place it on a very high pedestal ia the halls of dramatic art. No more damning indictment of the Smart Set has ever been written, and curiously enough the slaves of that sat have enjoyed the play quite as much. as the humbler-placed theatre-goer. The story is too• well-known to require re-telling here, and it is pre- :. sentecl with real forco by Mr. Arthur Bourcluer'e Company. Mr. Alfred Goddard gives a finished and; powerful interpretation of the part of Jack Frobisher, millionaire squatter who has married into the Smarts Set and learnt to hate its heartless frivolity and sham: with an intense hatred which eventually bubbles over. His ultimate revolt is obvious from the start, and when he does let himself go and damns the whole shallow system iii which he and Lady Alethea have been so aimlessly revolving the audience cheers enthusiasticality. In fact, the frequent' " hear hears " as Frobisher speaks out were a tribute alike to the author and to Mr.Gothlard's acting,. Miss Nancy Beresford makes a charming Lady Alethea Frobisher, and one cannot help feeling pleased that she evidences the possession of a .heart underneath the light and superfichil exterior which suffices for the social necessities of Mayfair. Frobisher tears her away before her nature is absolutely ruined. Miss Beres ford well paurtrays the natural spirit of revolt, and her ultimate submission is artistically done. The scene between her and the debonair Dallas is capital, and illustrates the fondness of a woman for playing with fire regardless of the certainty that she will get her fingers.burnt. The part of Dallas is riot an envi- able one, but it is cleverly presented by Mr. A. W. Tyrer. Miss Elsie Ross, as Lady Lucy Darenham, plays the ingenue very artistically. One of the cleverest things in the play is the caricature of decayed nobility in the person of the Marquis of Steyenton• The part is one which requires skilled handling, and we can honestly say that Mr. Ben. Lewin does it full justice. His stormy interview with Frobisher was splendidly presented, and the roars of laughter must have been ample reward to Mr. Lewin. We have not seen a better Hankey Bannister than that of Mr. Russell ' Barry, who is just" . sufficiently rough and unsophisticated to make the necessary contrast to the smart set which welcomes him for his money. The group of ladies who forra ' the Lady Alethea's private circle —Miss Marnington,i The Duckess of Skye and Lady Parchester —are -t„ fascinating with their drollery of speech and personal elegance. Miss Pauline Strans'displays real talent and makes the most of her opportunities for smartness as Miss Mernington, while Miss Millie Einden,personatas the card-sharping Duchess perfectly in the famous bridge scene. As the epigrammatic Bertram Hanna ford, Mr. George Percy seems hardly sufficiently con- versant with the part to give the drwery speeches a- natural instead of a studied air. Miss Ormonde. Wynne is both dignified and charming as Lady Westerby, and the numerous minor parts are all in capable hands. The play is most tastefully mounted, and the dresses of the ladies have a never-failing interest for the members of the fair sex in tl; audience.

The stirring and powerful drama "The Convict'a Daughter" will commence its third visit to the Court Theatre, Warrington, on Monday next. On each of its previous appearances good business has been attracted. Lovers of melodrama may auticipate 3 capital performance as Mr. Frank Bertram again, assumes the title role of Michael Graham "the tramp,' . .
the part he has now played over two thousand tinoies. In the third act a most sensational incident will he witnessed, the convict jumping on to an express train. in his escape from prison.

Sr. THOMAS'S Mr's CLASS.—.About 70 members and friends of Et. Thomas's Men's Class (B section) spent e very pleasant evening in the school on Thursday. Games of various kinds were indulged in and carried out with spirit, the Vicar, who was present part of the evening, joining in them as heartily as any. At ten o'clock the party gathered for a fere parting words from the teacher, Mr. Hallows. Votes of thanks were passed. The evening hymn was sung and, all departed pleased with the evening's enjoyment. ST. THOMAS'S BAND OF HOPE.—The opening meet- ing of the above took place on Wednesday evening. There was a good muster of members old and new. The superintendent, Mr. J. Hallows, pointed out the lines oe which they hoped to work for this season. Their object was to teach the children kindness, temperance and love to all around them. The Vicar will give the first. ddress nest week.

Labour Bureau. During September 214 fresh applicants registered as compared with 218 during September, 1907. Forty-seven situations were offered by employers as compared with 31, and 40 situations were filed through the bureau as against GO situations duriim: September, 1901. There are now on the register out of employment 300 persons in the following trades : Building trade, 8; iron trade, 40 ; wire trade, 11 ; horsemen, 11; clerks and warehousemen, 4; general labourers, 53 ; men for miscellaneous occupations. 41; lads and youths, 51; women for charring and daily work, 51; domestic servants, 15; women for mis- cellaneous occupations, 23 ; girls under 13 years old, 31. The general depression of trade continues,and many of the large works are still running short time. Through 'the lack of co-operation of some of the trade unions in not registering it would be difficult to ascertain with any amount of certainty the actual number of persons who are unemployed, but it is generally believed that there must be at least 1,000 persons unemployed in Warrington at the present time. Fortunately the present fine weather is giving a better opportunity to the outside workers of continuing ja their employment.

div.head: Death _of _an Indian Mutiny Veteran.
div.p: Death _of _an Indian Mutiny Veteran.

The death occurred on Sutnray, after a very long illness, of Mr. John Kieff, 40, Cairo-street, at the age of 83 years. Mr. Kieff was at one time a sergeant of the Militia under the command of the late Colonel Ireland Blackburne and Colonel Godfrey. He had seen much active service and took part in the quelling of the Punjab and Indian Mutinies. On retiring from active military work, he occupied the post as caretaker at the mess-room of the officers of his late regiment, which is now known as the Masonic Hall in Bold-street. On the death of his wife he went to live with Mr. Daley, St. Austin's-lane, who has had care of him for five years. For a considerable time be had been confined to his bed. Mr. Kieff in his early life was a fine specimen of manhood, and enjoyed good health The funeral took place on Wednesday at the Warring ton Cemetery. A detachment of the South Lancashire Regiment accompanied the hearse and en route the hand played the "Dead March." After the coffin was lowered into the grave three volleys were fired as last tribute to the dead hero. The " Last Post" was also sounded.

COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER. IVOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next 1.1 GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER vsill be holden at the COURT-HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 19th day of OCTOBER, 1908, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Altrincham, Bucklow, Dukinfield, Middlewich, Sandbach, Congleton, Northwich, Prestbury and Stockport, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Divisions, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the COURT HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 19th day of OCTOBER NEXT, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the CASTLE OF CHESTER on WEDNESDAY the 28th day of OCTOBER, 1908, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Broxton, Cheater Castle, Daresbury, Eddisbury, Nantv.ich, Runcorn, Winsford and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last- mentioned Divisions will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, at the Opening of the Court on WEDNES- DAY, the 28th day of OCTOBER, 1908, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County Palatine of Chester. Chester, 29th September, 1908.

P. —Goals— Parochial St.L'arnabas' 2 ... 2 ... 0 ... 0 ... 4 ... 0 ... 4 lleathside Wycliffe 3 . 2 . 0 . 1 . 4 ... 3 ... 4 Trinity St. James' I 1 1 1 ... 3 ... 2 ... 3 Hamilton st 3 1 ... 1 ... 1 ... 6 ... 0 ... :3 Christ Church 3 ... 0 ... 1 ... 2 ... 4 ... 15 ... 1 Silver street 1 ... 0 ... 0 ... 1 ... 1 ... 5 ... 0 Ar p 1 ey-street 2 0 ... 0 ... 2 ... 1 ... 13 ... 0 St. Alban's St. Mary's 1 .. 0 0 ... 1 ... 0 ... 5 ... 0 Beamont Christ Church boys visited the Parochial enclosure and went down very badly before a heavier and smarter team by 10-1. The inside-right and left half played particularly well for the winners, while the visitors' left-back played a sterling game. The weak spot of the losers was at, right- back, from which place all the goals came. Challiuor as centre did not feed his wings sufficiently, but attempted to much "on his own." Later in the week better form was displayed in the match with Hamilton-street, and the result was a draw. Parochial boys after their Christ Church victory visited Arpley-street, and meeting with no opposition scored ton goals. Even the victors, however, showed little science. St. James' and Wycliffe met on the ground of the former, and a fast, keen game was witnessed. Wycliffe i scored n the last few minutes and thus gained two more points. The winners' form was most gratifying after their trying experiences last season. The losers were somewhat unlucky not to clivide the points. St. Mary's opened their season eisnstronsly, going , down before the onslaughts of the Trinity boys by 5-0. O'Neill was the mainstay of the winners both in attack and defence. The losers combined well but had little idea of shooting. • Funeral of Miss Lenin Warburtan. The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Saturday of \ liss Lettice Warburton, daughter of Mr. Benjamin Warburton, of 18, Elaine-street, whose death occurred the previous Tuesday under touching circumstances. She was only 13 years of age, and gave promise of a successful career in the educational world. In April last she passed the preliminary certificate examination with distinction in history, and arrangements had been made for her to proceed to Edge Hill Training College, Liverpool, when it was fouud on medical examination, that an operation to the throat was necessary. This was successfully per- formed, but later other ailments developed, to which she succumbed,to the great regret of all who knew her. There was a large gathering at the Cemetery,and before the cortege left the house a couple of hymns were effectively rendered. Almost the whole of the pupil I teachers and pupils attending the Secondary School I were present. The members of the Juvenile Order cf Bechabites also walked in procession. Hundreds of people, young and cld, assembled at the graveside, lincluding a large number of the congregation attend- ing the Brick-street Independent Methodist Church, !where Miss Warburton was a worshipper. The ser- vice was conducted by Mr. Thomas Wright and Mr. James Shaw, and a hyrnu was also sung at the graveside. Numerous floral tributes wete received, including one from the teachers and pupils at the Secondary School, and one from the Juvenile Order of Rechabites.
